World.title: Lives on landmines: Zim’s long road to a safer land
World.content:
Opinion

Vanessa Gonye · October 23, 2026

HE lost not one, but both legs to deadly landmines scattered across his community.

Such is the tragic story of Kenias Chihumo (83), who lives under Chief Chirambadeya in Mudzi district and has endured nearly four decades of life with a disability caused by landmine explosions.

According to Chihumo, his first accident occurred in 1988.

Thirteen years later, in 2001, he suffered a second explosion along the Mudze River in Mudzi, at the same location as the first incident.

Having lost both lower limbs, he now moves around on his knees.

“I was doing some farming in my garden, which is close to the river, where I would fetch water to use,” he said.

“That is when I stepped on it at the bank of the river.”

In 2001, he suffered a similar ordeal while farming along the same river, stepping on another landmine.

“In 2001, I encountered the same accident and was taken to Harare Central Hospital (now Sally Mugabe Central Hospital) for treatment,” he said.

Life was never the same for Chihumo, whose injuries left him without both legs.

An estimated three million anti-personnel landmines were laid between 1974 and 1979, creating dense minefields along Zimbabwe’s borders.

Since independence in 1980, between 1 500 and 1 700 people have reportedly been killed or injured, while more than 120 000 cattle have been lost.

Chihumo is among those whose lives have been profoundly affected by the country’s landmine legacy.

For survivors, the consequences extend far beyond the physical injuries, often bringing lasting emotional and financial hardship.

“My life has been suffering since I became disabled,” Chihumo said.

His elderly wife now takes on menial work, including farming and other odd jobs in the community, to ensure the family has something to eat at the end of the day.

Despite his circumstances, Chihumo puts on a brave face and appears to have come to terms with his fate, painful as it remains.

Another landmine survivor, Daniel Kutsakatika (39), of Jurimani village, said counselling had helped him cope with the abrupt changes to his life after losing a leg in an explosion.

Kutsakatika was on his way home from work when he stepped on a landmine.

Since that day, life has been difficult for the father of six, who must provide for his large family, which includes his two wives.

“I was coming from doing my job as a herdsman, holding my child,” he said.

“I didn’t feel anything at first, but just found myself on the ground.

“My companion started to panic and I told him not to worry, but to carry me home.”

Kutsakatika said he sought assistance at a nearby clinic before being referred to Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals for further treatment.

His leg was subsequently amputated.

“From the incident to date, my life has never been the same.

“I am struggling to take care of my family.”

The ordeal left him traumatised, although he tries to reassure those around him that he is coping.

He broke down in tears midway through the interview, revealing the lasting emotional impact of the incident.

“I received counselling, which was really helpful and I have accepted the new life,” he said.

“Another challenge is that my artificial leg is quite worn out and it is making life difficult for me.

“It is my wish to get assistance to start a project so I may increase income for my family.”

Despite his struggles, Kutsakatika welcomed the ongoing de-mining exercise in the area, which is nearing completion.

He said the operation would help give residents a greater sense of security, as many continue to live in fear of becoming victims of landmine explosions.

For now, he said, the threat remains real, with landmines still scattered across the community.

Addressing a gathering during a high-level field visit to mine-affected communities under Project RECLAIM in Mudzi, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) resident representative Ayodele Odusola said about 700 landmines had been discovered and destroyed in the district.

“Because of this partnership, we have real results to show since our work began in January 2026,” he said.

“Here in Mudzi, since April 2026, MAG has made over 80 000 square metres of land safe. Almost 700 landmines have been found and destroyed.

“In Rushinga, between February and October 2026, The HALO Trust has cleared nearly 93 000 square metres of land. It has found and destroyed over 1 800 landmines.”

Odusola said the combined area cleared in the two districts exceeded 173 000 square metres.

“That is about the size of 24 football pitches, now safe for families to farm, to graze their cattle and to walk on. Over 2 500 landmines that will never again take a life, a leg or a cow,” he said.

In a speech read on her behalf by Defence deputy minister Levi Mayihlome, Defence minister Oppah Muchinguri-Kashiri acknowledged that landmines continued to pose a threat to people living in border areas.

“The government recognises that landmines continue to threaten lives, restrict access to productive land and undermine livelihoods in affected communities,” she said.

“The government will therefore continue to mobilise resources to accelerate mine clearance and promote inclusive development.”

Since clearance operations began in February 2026, Project RECLAIM has made progress in both

districts.

By September 2026, the project had cleared 92 353 square metres in Rushinga district and destroyed 1 833 landmines, against a target of 122 500 square metres.

In Mudzi, the project aims to clear 110 000 square metres by completion.

Meanwhile, UNDP-funded mine-action operations have released 80 941 square metres of land and recovered and destroyed 694 anti-personnel mines.

The project is funded by the Government of Japan and UNDP. Japan committed US$2 946 582,32, while UNDP is contributing US$400 000 towards its implementation.

The project began in August 2025 and is scheduled to run until December 2028.

For communities in Mudzi and Rushinga, every square metre cleared represents more than a project statistic. It is land that families can use to grow food, graze cattle and travel with less fear.

For survivors such as Chihumo and Kutsakatika, de-mining cannot reverse the injuries they have s

uffered.

But it can help protect others from similar tragedies, restore access to productive land, support livelihoods and uphold the dignity of those living with the consequences of Zimbabwe’s landmine legacy.

World.title: Patients first: Why ZADHR supports the medical aid reforms
World.content:
Opinion

ZADHR · October 23, 2026

PAYING for medical aid should bring peace of mind, not the fear of being unable to afford treatment when illness strikes.

Yet for many Zimbabweans, making monthly contributions does not guarantee that their medical expenses will be fully covered.

When the hospital bill arrives, patients and their families may still be left struggling to meet the shortfall.

At the heart of this problem lies a fundamental question: should a medical aid society that collects members’ contributions to finance their healthcare also own and operate hospitals, pharmacies and other facilities from which healthcare is purchased?

When the same institution controls the funding and competes to provide the service, conflict of interest can arise, patient choice can be constrained and the interests of members risk being pushed aside.

The Zimbabwe Association of Doctors for Human Rights (ZADHR) supports the proposed reforms to separate the financing of healthcare from its provision.

This is not simply a debate about business ownership.

It is about accountability for members’ contributions, fairness in the healthcare market, the quality-of-care patients receive and the protection of the right to healthcare under section 76 of the Constitution of Zimbabwe.

Medical aid must put patients first.

The proposed reforms offer an opportunity to restore that principle by ensuring that medical aid societies focus on financing members’ healthcare, while independent providers compete to deliver the care patients need.

With appropriate safeguards and a carefully managed transition, Zimbabwe can move towards a system that places patients’ interests, dignity and access to good quality healthcare at its centre.

Where we are today

Medical aid covers a small and shrinking share of Zimbabweans.

Industry figures presented to Parliament in April put coverage at about 8% of the population, with more than 90% paying for care out of their own pockets.

Members typically contribute between US$55 and US$65 a month.

Over the past two decades, the largest societies have become much more than funders.

They have bought or built hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, imaging centres, dental practices and ambulance services.

Researchers at EQUINET documented this as early as 2010.

They found that most acquisitions were existing facilities rather than adding new capacity to the health system.

Instead of containing costs, as promised, the move coincided with rising costs.

In practice, a single society can now sit on both sides of almost every step in a patient’s care.

It holds the money, writes the price list, approves or rejects claims and owns facilities that compete with the very providers it pays.

Independent doctors, hospitals and pharmacies must, therefore, negotiate their fees with, and wait to be paid by, a direct competitor.

This creates a structural conflict of interest, even where the people making decisions act in good faith.

Patients who cannot cover the gap often end up in already overstretched public hospitals.

The cost of this arrangement is, therefore, carried by the whole health system, not only by medical aid members.

Meanwhile, reimbursement rates in many schemes have not kept pace with the real cost of running a practice, which inflation, currency instability and imported equipment and consumables have all pushed up.

When a society pays less than care actually costs, the difference does not vanish.

It is passed on to the patient as a shortfall and too often the provider, not the payer, is held responsible.

What the reform proposes

The Health and Child Care ministry has proposed amending section 14 of the Medical Services (Medical Aid Societies) Regulations, 2000, SI 330/2000, as amended by (SI 35/2004 and SI 58/2025) the regulations that govern medical aid societies.

The amendment would bar societies from owning or operating healthcare facilities such as hospitals, clinics and pharmacies.

Societies would return to their core function: pooling members’ contributions and purchasing care on their behalf. Those that already own facilities would be required to divest.

The proposal has been before Parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Health, which heard submissions from the industry in April 2026.

Funders, led by the Association of Healthcare Funders of Zimbabwe and Cimas Health Group, have campaigned hard against it.

Civil society organisations, including the Community Working Group on Health, and many doctors have spoken in its favor.

Why ZADHR supports the reform

Medical aid exists to finance care, not to build business empires

Contributions are paid to protect members when they fall ill, and societies hold non-profit status for exactly that reason.

Keeping sensible reserves is responsible management.

Using members’ contributions as capital for commercial expansion, without giving those members any ownership or say, is something else entirely.

The conflict of interest is structural, not personal

A society that owns clinics has every incentive to steer members towards its own facilities, and to pay independent providers less.

It can approve claims quickly at its own pharmacy and slowly elsewhere or treat its own laboratory as the default.

EQUINET’s research found that only 11% of plans fully reimbursed services from providers outside the society’s own network.

That is not managed care; it is managed choice.

Patient choice and continuity of care suffer

Patients with chronic illnesses, pregnancies or cancer often need a doctor they trust over many years.

When a society nudges or forces members towards its own facilities, that relationship is broken.

Choice of provider is not a luxury. It is part of good, safe medicine.

Quality must be judged by outcomes, not throughput

A facility can treat large numbers of patients and still deliver poor care if consultations are rushed and staff are stretched thin.

When the payer owns the provider, no independent party checks whether members receive the standard of care their contributions pay for.

A purchaser that stands apart from providers can set and enforce standards across all of them, from waiting times and staffing to clinical results.

Fair competition protects patients Independent doctors, hospitals and pharmacies are being squeezed out, especially in smaller towns.

Fewer independent providers means fewer options, longer distances and, ultimately, higher prices.

Smaller medical aid societies, which do not own facilities, are also disadvantaged against vertically integrated rivals.

Claims of lower costs have never been independently verified

Integrated societies say their own facilities are cheaper.

If that is true, the evidence should be published and independently audited so that members, regulators and Parliament can judge it for themselves.

So far, it has not been. Because societies are spending money that belongs to their members, the burden of proof rests with them.

Shortfalls are a policy choice, not a law of nature

A scheme whose premiums rise with costs, but whose reimbursement rates lag behind them, will always leave members with a gap.

When that same scheme also earns revenue from its own facilities, the incentive to fix its rates weakens.

Removing the ownership link pushes societies to compete on what members value most: how fully and fairly they pay for care.

Good governance requires clear lines

The sector has suffered serious governance scandals, including revelations in 2014 of extraordinary executive pay at one of the largest societies.

Complex group structures, with subsidiaries spanning hospitals, pharmacies and property, make oversight harder for members and regulators alike.

A society that only funds care is far easier to supervise.

This is international best practice

Separating the purchaser of care from the provider is a widely used principle of health financing.

It is also the foundation on which Zimbabwe must build a fair National Health Insurance scheme.

Getting the private funding market right now prepares the ground for universal health coverage.

Answering the industry’s objections

The funders have warned of a “collapse cascade” if the reform passes. Their concerns deserve a serious answer.

“Without our facilities, tariffs and premiums will rise.”

Societies already have a powerful tool to control costs: the tariffs they negotiate and the claims they approve.

A strong, independent purchaser can bargain hard with every provider. It does not need to own the hospital to do so.

If integration truly lowered costs, the savings should already show in lower premiums and fewer shortfalls. Members do not see them.

“We built facilities because the market failed.”

Medicine shortages and tariff inflation are real problems.

The answer is better regulation, strategic purchasing and stronger public facilities, not turning funders into competitors.

A temporary fix for market failure has become a permanent conflict of interest.

“Kaiser Permanente and Bupa do it.”

These organisations operate in markets with strong, independent regulators, transparent accounts and enforceable consumer protections.

Zimbabwe has only just placed medical aid societies under the Insurance and Pensions Commission (IPEC), through section 2 of the Insurance and Pensions Commission Amendment Act of 2026 gazetted in April 2026, and that oversight is still being built.

Copying the business model before the safeguards are proven is a risk to members, not a reform.

“Jobs and services will be lost.”

Divestment does not mean closure. A clinic sold to independent doctors, a nursing group or an investor continues to employ staff and treat patients.

What changes is who owns it, and whether its owner also controls the purse.

A phased, supervised transition can protect both jobs and continuity of care.

ZADHR agrees with the industry on one point: the reform should be implemented carefully, with a sensible transition period and independent oversight.

What we ask of Parliament and the ministry

ZADHR urges Parliament and the Ministry of Health and Child Care to:

lPass the amendment prohibiting medical aid societies from owning or operating healthcare facilities.

lSet a clear, phased divestment timeline, with protection for staff and continuity of care for patients.

lMake IPEC’s new oversight count. The Insurance and Pensions Commission Amendment Act of 2026 places medical aid societies under IPEC under section 2.

lIPEC must be resourced to audit societies and their subsidiaries, enforce solvency and protect members, working hand in hand with the ministry on standards of care.

lRequire transparent reporting, including audited accounts, claims ratios and how reserves are invested, published annually for members.

lReview the tariff framework so that reimbursement reflects the real cost of care, ending the shortfall trap for patients.

lProtect members’ choice of provider, so that no member is penalised for seeing a doctor or facility of their choice.

Zimbabweans who pay into medical aid are entitled to know that their contributions are used to pay for their care, and for nothing else.

Separating the funding of care from its provision is a simple, well-established principle that protects that promise.

ZADHR urges Parliament to adopt it, and to return the patient to the centre of a system that exists to serve them.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: As Ebola Spreads to 8th DR Congo Province, Families Battle to Feed Themselves
World.content:
A health worker carries a stretcher into an Ebola treatment centre in the DR Congo.

Geneva — Hunger in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) is undermining efforts to combat Ebola as the deadly disease has expanded across borders and also to an eighth province of the huge central African country, the UN said on Friday.

Families facing Ebola in the DR Congo, which has a population of more than 105 million, can find that protecting themselves from the virus can also mean losing the means to feed their children, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

“Today, the outbreak has spread to an eighth province, reaching communities already under immense pressure,” David Stevenson, the WFP's DRC country director, said during a UN press conference.

“As it spreads, hunger continues to undermine the measures needed to contain it.”

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

And earlier in the week, the World Health Organisation (WHO), on Oct. 20, said that Nigeria has confirmed one imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

It became the fifth country to detect the virus since the DRC declared an outbreak on May 15.

The spread of the disease comes as agencies fighting the escalating Ebola virus in the DRC constantly battle to win the trust of local communities, according to international groups in the field calling for the protection of health workers.

Stevenson said that the WFP has two critical roles: helping families seek care without sacrificing food and providing the logistics backbone that keeps the wider response moving.

“Without sustained support, we risk leaving families unable to follow health guidance when it matters most.”

The WFP official explained that in Ituri’s Mungbwalu, the epicentre of the outbreak, Francine Birungi Amoti has lost a child to Ebola.

“She is raising her six surviving children and another baby entrusted to her care. Violence has cut her off from her fields.

“She told me, ‘If you go, you may not even return alive, and I do not have money to buy food at the local market. So we stay at home, and WFP helps us enormously.’”

For Francine, food assistance means feeding the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life.

'INSECURITY AND HUNGER'

“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger,” said Stevenson.

He also cited the case in North-Kivu’s Butembo, where Isabelle Kyakimwa arrived at an Ebola treatment centre without strength.

“As she recovered, she told us: ‘Food is important for us as patients because it helps us regain the strength to keep going.’

Close 

Her words show what food assistance brings to a treatment centre: regular, safe, nutritious meals that support recovery, dignity, and continuity of care.

“Food does not treat Ebola. Medical teams do,” said Stevenson.

“But their work takes place amid severe food insecurity and continued violence that repeatedly displaces families, destroys livelihoods and complicates access to care.”

He said food assistance is vital to supporting patients through that care and that WFP needs $115 million over the next six months, including $79 million for hot meals and dry rations.

World.title: Kenya: Calls for Penalties Follow 12-Story Building Collapse
World.content:
A building under construction collapsed in the Eastleigh neighborhood of Nairobi.

Nairobi — Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has called for tougher penalties against rogue developers and the restoration of prosecutorial powers to county governments following the collapse of an incomplete 12-storey building in Eastleigh.

Sakaja said weak penalties for violating construction regulations undermine enforcement efforts and allow developers to compromise building safety, putting lives at risk.

Speaking as he led multi-agency rescue operations at the site along 1st Avenue, 9th Street, the Governor urged professional bodies representing architects, engineers and quantity surveyors to take action against developers who dismiss qualified experts after obtaining construction approvals.



He said some developers engage licensed professionals to secure approvals but subsequently remove them from projects and proceed with construction using unqualified personnel, undermining safeguards intended to ensure buildings meet approved designs and safety standards.

"We have formally written to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and we hope our request will be considered. Counties must be empowered to take firm action against rogue developers who disregard building regulations and put lives at risk," Sakaja said.

The Governor questioned the deterrent effect of existing penalties, noting that some developers found guilty of violating construction regulations could face fines as low as Sh5,000.

"Even when such offenders are arrested and taken to court, the penalties can be as low as Sh5,000, which is not a sufficient deterrent," he said.

Sakaja argued that restoring prosecutorial powers to county governments would strengthen enforcement and enable authorities to take firmer action against developers who disregard approved construction plans and safety requirements.

He called on professional associations representing architects, engineers, quantity surveyors and builders to collaborate with county governments in identifying and investigating cases where qualified professionals are withdrawn from construction sites under questionable circumstances.

The Governor said the bodies should take appropriate disciplinary action against professionals found culpable, adding that experts responsible for building design, supervision and safety must be allowed to discharge their duties without interference.

Sakaja also reiterated the need for developers to obtain occupation certificates before putting buildings into use. He said structures must undergo the necessary inspections to establish that they are safe and fit for occupation.

According to the Governor, developers are required to secure county approvals, engage qualified professionals and sign indemnity forms committing them to comply with approved plans and construction standards.

However, he said some developers disregard these commitments after obtaining approvals, compromising the integrity of construction projects.

The calls for stronger enforcement came after an incomplete 12-storey building collapsed in Eastleigh, triggering a multi-agency search and rescue operation amid fears that people were trapped beneath the rubble.

The building was still under construction, with the ground floor occupied at the time of the collapse.

Nairobi City County emergency response teams were coordinating operations alongside the National Disaster Operations Centre, the Kenya Red Cross, the Kenya Defence Forces and other agencies.

Heavy machinery had been deployed to clear debris and create access to sections where victims could be trapped, as additional resources were mobilised to support the rescue effort.

Sakaja urged families and members of the public with information about missing persons to report to designated centres established by rescue teams at the scene.

Close 

Residents were also advised to share information through the county's emergency hotlines, 1508 and 1199.

"Our health teams are on standby to provide immediate medical attention and support rescue efforts as soon as victims are reached. We are doing everything possible to ensure the operation proceeds as quickly and safely as possible," he said.

The collapse has renewed scrutiny of building safety enforcement in Nairobi, particularly compliance with approved construction plans, the engagement of qualified professionals and inspections at different stages of development.

Sakaja said stronger legal powers, tougher penalties and closer collaboration between county governments and professional bodies were necessary to hold developers accountable and prevent similar incidents.

He maintained that restoring county prosecutorial powers would complement existing inspection and enforcement mechanisms by strengthening the ability of local authorities to pursue violations of construction regulations.

World.title: Rwanda: Kagame Defends Strict Dress Codes Amid Rwanda's Dressing Controversy
World.content:
Rwandan President Paul Kagame has defended cultural expectations on dressing, arguing that societies have their own standards of acceptable behaviour which should not be abandoned simply because other countries embrace different ways of life.

Speaking on Thursday while addressing more than 10,000 young Rwandans at BK Arena in Kigali during the "Meet The President" session, Kagame said dress codes should be understood within the context of the places people visit and the values of the society in which they live.

"If you are going to the beach, by the water, where people go to relax, there is a certain way you can dress and behave that may be different from other places. That is perfectly acceptable. But imagine someone coming here dressed as though they were at the beach. Would that work? Wouldn't you all turn around and wonder, what happened to this person?" Kagame asked.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

His remarks come amid a growing debate in Rwanda over restrictions on women's dressing, following incidents in which women have faced scrutiny over their clothing in public spaces.

The debate intensified after a video circulated showing police officers forcefully handcuffing a young woman wearing a miniskirt at a bus park in Rubavu.

The Rwanda National Police subsequently cleared the woman of wrongdoing and detained the officers involved pending disciplinary review.

The incident also drew criticism from human rights advocates and public commentators, who argued that cultural values should not be used to justify police intimidation, harassment or arbitrary enforcement of dress standards against women.

Addressing the wider debate, Kagame said the expectations should apply to men as well, arguing that discussions about dressing are often unfairly directed at women.

"By the way, this is not just about women. Most of the time, these things are made to be about women, but the same applies to men. Even now, imagine we are sitting here, and a man suddenly walks in, as though he has just come from the gym, wearing shorts, with nothing on his upper body, and comes to sit among us. People would ask, what happened to this person? Did he forget where he was going?" he said.

Kagame argued that societies should be allowed to maintain their own social standards rather than adopt practices from other countries without considering whether they fit local values.

He said people's willingness to participate in a particular social setting could also depend on the expectations established by those organising it.

"Now, if we had all agreed to come dressed that way, then perhaps that is how it would be. But some people would not come. Isn't that so? Some would simply decide not to attend, saying, we are not going to be part of that," he said.

The Rwandan leader said communities have ways of regulating behaviour through shared expectations and self-regulation, adding that practices accepted elsewhere should not automatically be embraced by Rwandans.

"There is a way society regulates itself, including through self-regulation. But when you simply say, we have seen this elsewhere, so let us do the same here, and you bring it into our society, society may tell you, we have not reached that point yet. Perhaps we were moving in that direction, but we are not there yet," Kagame said.

He called for disagreements over cultural values to be handled through dialogue rather than hostility, saying people should be able to reach an understanding when differences emerge.

"That should not create any hostility. There should be a way of regulating these things so that people can come to an understanding," he said.

Kagame compared society's response to unfamiliar practices to the body's reaction to a foreign object, which it gradually attempts to remove.

"It is like a foreign body. I think those of you in the medical profession know this. When a foreign object, a fragment of something, enters the body, the body tends to reject it. It keeps pushing it out. Even when a thorn gets stuck in your skin, if you leave it there for some time, it begins to work its way out. Eventually, you find it near the surface and remove it. Society works in much the same way," he said.

He added that tensions can arise when individuals seek to introduce practices that conflict with the established values of a community, while other members of that society resist the changes.

"A healthy society, with its own way of functioning, when something unfamiliar is introduced into it, gradually, little by little, that society begins to push it away. There is then a struggle between someone trying to change society to fit something they have brought from elsewhere, and society itself saying, do not bring these things here, and pushing that person away. But there should be no conflict. That is how these things should work," Kagame said.

Close 

He urged young people to reflect on the values they want for themselves and the direction in which they want their society to develop.

"Young people like you should keep these things in mind. Think about them. Understand what it is that you want for yourselves," he said.

Kagame also called for open discussions about changing social norms, urging young Rwandans to question practices that are becoming more common but which they consider inconsistent with their culture or harmful to society.

"Even here, in our discussions, people should be able to raise these questions and say, there are things we have seen becoming increasingly accepted in our society, yet they are not part of our culture. They do not even bring us any benefit. Why should we accept them, especially when they are things that harm people? Why?" he asked.

World.title: Nigeria: Health Is Economic Infrastructure - Why Nigeria Must Invest in Health
World.content:
blog

Listen to this article 8 min The recently concluded World Health Summit in Berlin, themed "From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health", reinforced a key message: health spending is an investment, not just an expense. Yet Nigeria's 2026 Appropriation Bill proposed ₦2.48 trillion for health out of ₦58.47 trillion, about 4.2% of the budget. That is less than a third of the 15% target African governments agreed to in the 2001 Abuja Declaration.

Closing this gap requires recognising health as an investment in economic growth, much like roads and power. Nigeria's growth ambitions depend on people being healthy enough to participate in the economy. Health should therefore be treated as economic infrastructure in the country's development priorities and budget decisions.

What the evidence actually supports



Egypt's experience illustrates the potential economic returns of health investment. At the summit session Funding the Future: Unlocking the Economic and Fiscal Returns of Health Innovation, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Egypt's Minister of Health and Population, described a $240 million early-detection programme reaching 60 million people, followed by affordable generic treatment. It was projected to save $7 billion by 2030, a 688% return.

However, these are projections, not a confirmed result. For Nigeria, achieving comparable gains would require screening capacity and reliable medicine supplies that are not yet available at the same scale. Martin Seychell, Deputy Director-General at DG INTPA at the European Commission, cautioned that better outcomes depend on how the money is spent.

"We should not make the mistake of simply gauging and assessing efforts simply on the basis of how much money we are investing in health budgets. Because we know, of course, if you underinvest, you will not get good outcomes. But it doesn't follow that if you just increase the health budgets without a clear strategy, you will get better outcomes."

Nigeria's clearest return is household income

One of the clearest benefits for Nigeria is the funds families could keep if healthcare were more affordable. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO, Amref Health Africa singled out Nigeria when discussing the high out-of-pocket health expenditure, noting that what people pay out of pocket is "ridiculously higher than the government spends."

People pay about 71.9% of current health expenditure out of pocket. An analysis of the 2023/24 General Household Survey found that 45.5% of households faced catastrophic health spending, meaning health costs accounted for at least 10% of their household budget. These bills can force families to borrow, sell belongings or cut spending on food and education.

During the Strategic Health Economy session, Dr Ezekwesili recalled that evidence showing that malaria cost Africa about 2% of its GDP "changed the conversation" with ministers and described the disease as a "productivity tax on the economies." The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare estimates that malaria reduces Nigeria's GDP by more than $1.1 billion each year, while Nigeria accounts for 27% of global cases.

At the same session, Dr Satoshi Ezoe, Japan's Assistant Minister for Global Health, explained that Japan reached universal health coverage in 1961 while still recovering from the Second World War, and argued that "we laid the foundation by making UHC, which led to socioeconomic development."

Nigeria is one of the first eight countries in the UHC Knowledge Hub, a Japanese initiative with the World Health Organization and the World Bank that brings health and finance ministries together to plan for universal coverage. Successful coverage should mean fewer families are pushed into hardship by medical bills and fewer workdays lost, not enrolment figures alone.

Who captures the value?

The economic case for health investment extends to building local industries and creating employment opportunities. Yet Africa captures little of the value from the health products it uses, as Dr Obiageli Ezekwesili, founder and chief executive officer of Human Capital Africa, told the summit during the session The Strategic Health Economy:

"[Africa's] capacity in terms of... global manufacturing... it's less than 5%. Then you look at... competitiveness... how much value does Africa gain from the health value chain -- also insignificant...

Nigeria aims to increase local production of essential health products to 70% by 2030. The Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain is supported by tax and duty waivers on pharmaceutical inputs and about $2 billion in financing commitments.

However, packaging imported products locally is not the same as making them locally. Manufacturers still rely on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients to produce medicines, leaving them exposed to foreign-exchange fluctuations and price volatility.

Local production also needs skilled workers, as does the wider health system. Nigeria has 95,456 registered doctors but only 60,551 with active practising licenses, while its 2024 National Policy on Health Workforce Migration requires wider implementation.

The role of policy in enabling health workers to deliver care also features in the summit session Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century, where Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO of Amref Health Africa, stressed its importance for community health workers.

Making investment accountable

Funding also must reach the services it is meant for. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Gitahi warned that prevention and vaccination budgets "are the first to be cut" when fiscal space tightens, because their results are less visible.

Nigeria shows the risk: in 2025, only ₦36 million of the ₦218 billion appropriated for federal health capital projects was released. For Nigeria, the value of health investment lies in the industries it builds and the workers it equips. Realising that value requires funding, procurement and regulation to support these goals.

Close 

The following steps could help put this into practice;

The Office of the Accountant-General and Budget Office should include health infrastructure in quarterly cash plans and publish how much funding is released.

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and state schemes should automatically enrol eligible conditional cash transfer beneficiaries and publish whether enrolment reduces their out-of-pocket spending. In addition, the NHIA, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), and state governments could consider offering qualified Nigerian manufacturers multi-year purchasing agreements with clear standards for price, quality, and delivery. Reliable demand would make it easier for manufacturers to invest.

Incentives under the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) and NAFDAC approval pathways should reward verified local production, including making ingredients and meeting quality standards. Annual reporting should show which products are replacing imports.

Health belongs in Nigeria's growth strategy for the same reason ports and power do: the economy depends on it. That case must be reflected in funding released on time, stronger local production and affordable, quality care. Nigeria needs to spend more on health, use the funds strategically and measure whether people and the economy are better off.

World.title: South Africa: How Nurses Are Learning to Administer the New HIV Prevention Injection
World.content:
South Africa's rollout of lenacapavir, a six-monthly HIV prevention injection, requires nurses to learn, adapt and find ways to make it work for patients.

After 26 years in nursing, Sister Keitumetse "Tumi" Senokwane still had something new to learn about giving injections.

The six-monthly HIV-prevention jab, lenacapavir, often referred to as just LEN, presented a unique challenge.

"You know, lenacapavir is different. As much as I've got experience with injections, the needle size is different from the subcutaneous (beneath the skin) injections we are used to, and the solution is quite thick," says Senokwane. "Because we were not used to it, the practical training helped us to get used to it." She practised withdrawing the yellow liquid, using cooking oil as a stand-in.



That kind of preparation matters because lenacapavir for HIV prevention is being introduced at a time when South Africa still has a substantial need for effective HIV prevention options. The country had an estimated 140 000 new HIV infections in 2025. Modelling suggests that scaling up lenacapavir to 1.4 million to 2.1 million initiations a year by 2030 could avert an average of 32 200 to 51 700 infections annually.

But realising lenacapavir's potential will depend on more than getting the injection into clinics. It also requires nurses to administer it correctly, answer patients' questions, and adapt services to their needs.

Getting to grips with lenacapavir

Senokwane is a professional nurse and site manager at Maria Rantho Community Health Centre and Phedisong 1 Clinic in Tshwane, which are participating in the Wits RHI Len4PrEP study.

"LEN4PrEP is an implementation research study, so looking at how we can deliver the product in a real-world setting," says study investigator Dr Catherine Martin.

The researchers recruited 1 544 participants between November 2025 and June 2026, with follow-up continuing until June 2027. The study began several months before South Africa's national rollout of lenacapavir on 5 June 2026, when the injection was launched at 360 public health facilities across six provinces.

By 8 October, 76 922 people had initiated LEN nationally, including 36 733 in 133 facilities in Gauteng, according to health department spokesperson Foster Mohale.

For Senokwane and her colleagues, administering lenacapavir meant learning a new HIV prevention method.

Nurses first had to complete a compulsory Nurse-Initiated Management of Antiretroviral Therapy (NIMART) course, which provides a theoretical foundation for managing HIV and antiretroviral treatment. This was followed by practical training in preparing and administering LEN.

Training also covered eligibility, side effects, HIV testing and counselling, with videos and clinical mentorship providing additional support.

Mohale says feedback from early-rollout clinics, nurses and patients would help the department refine its training and guidelines.

At the study clinics, nurses also had to adapt the service to patients' needs and fit the new injection method into existing care.

The one-stop shop

The Department of Health's lenacapavir implementation guidelines emphasise counselling clients on their HIV prevention options and helping them choose a method that suits their needs.

At the study clinics, nurses incorporated LEN into existing sexual and reproductive health services, allowing clients to access HIV prevention alongside services such as family planning and STI screening and treatment during a single visit.

"You will get all services in one room like a one-stop shop," says Senokwane.

"Maybe you are here for lenacapavir, but we also check whether you are on a family planning method. If not, we will give you information and provide a family planning method for you, where we screen you for STIs, and then if you've got some infections, we also treat you," she says.

The LEN4PrEP study also used a mobile clinic to bring HIV prevention and sexual and reproductive health services to young people in their communities.

"So many of our clients already know us. They know how we treat them and the quality of service we provide," she says.

Initial LEN consultations took longer as nurses explained the available prevention methods and how soon each would offer protection against HIV.

"We give you the information and explain how each method works, how long until it is effective. Participants would like to know when they are going to be protected from HIV if they take this specific method," says Senokwane.

At the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society's Long-Acting Antiretroviral Treatment Conference in Johannesburg in September, Wits RHI's Professor Saiqa Mullick, Director of Implementation Science, shared early findings from the LEN4PrEP study.

She reported that convenience was a major reason participants opted for the lenacapavir jab. They valued not having to take a daily pill or make frequent clinic visits, while the injection offered greater privacy for some. It also attracted people new to PrEP, alongside existing users seeking a method that better suited their lives.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, refers to antiretroviral medicines taken to prevent HIV infection. When used as prescribed, oral PrEP has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV infection from sex. For several years now, HIV prevention tablets have been widely available in South Africa's public healthcare system, although uptake has been somewhat muted with only around 350 000 people taking the tablets in mid-2025, according to estimates from Thembisa, the leading mathematical model of HIV in South Africa.

Of the 1 538 participants whose method choices were reported, 85.8% selected the lenacapavir shot, compared with 13.7% who selected the prevention pills and 0.5% who chose not to use PrEP.

"People want options that fit into their lives," Mullick told delegates.

Sticking the landing

Patients could also choose where in the body to receive the injections: the upper arm, buttocks, abdomen or thigh.

Among the 1 319 participants who started LEN, Mullick says approximately 50% of women preferred the buttocks, while about 51% of men preferred the upper arm. The ongoing study will explore both men and women's reasons for injection-site preferences.

For nurses, the challenge was to administer the injections correctly while making the process as efficient as possible.

Lenacapavir requires getting two injections during the same visit. Patients also need to take two lenacapavir tablets on the day of their first injections, followed by another two tablets 24 hours later. These tablets form part of the initiation dose before they continue with injections every six months.

Senokwane says a Wits RHI pharmacist taught her a way to withdraw the solution while keeping the vial upright, rather than turning it upside down.

"That was the best method for me because it worked faster," says Senokwane.

"So with that method, you pull up 1.5 ml of air into the syringe and inject the needle into the vial. [The syringe] draws at least one ml by itself, without assistance, which allows the nurse to multitask. And then you also save time because you are able to prepare two injections at the same time," she says.

But efficiency was only part of the learning curve. Because lenacapavir is a thick solution, it needs to be injected slowly.

"I wish I knew that you can't inject it fast," Senokwane said. The thick solution required a slower injection technique to reduce leakage.

Slow administration was included in nurses' initial training, but its importance in minimising leakage was reinforced as they gained practical experience and shared lessons with colleagues.

Dr Martin says that in the early stages of implementation, nurses consulted experts, including those involved in clinical trials, on how to manage leakage at the injection site.

"As local experience grew, they learnt to reassure participants that minor leakage could occur and to assess more substantial leakage to determine whether further follow-up was needed."

Answering patient concerns

Patients were also concerned about the side effects of lenacapavir.

Lumps or small nodules at the injection site are a common side effect of lenacapavir. In one clinical trial, which included 2 140 participants who received lenacapavir, roughly 64% developed subcutaneous nodules at the injection site.

"Most of the clients were curious about the nodules. They were worried about whether they would be able to continue with their normal activities, especially those who wanted to exercise," says Senokwane.

"They wanted to know how long the nodule would last and whether they would get another one when they came back for their second injection. Usually, by the time they came for their next injection, the nodule would have disappeared."

Others were worried about the pain.

"We advise them that if the nodule comes with pain, just use a warm or cold compress, or you can even use a painkiller," explains Senokwane.

Mullick says addressing these concerns and discussing them with clients in advance is part of making the injection work for patients in practice.

"This might seem something relatively small, but from an implementation perspective, it contributes considerably to the person receiving the product."

Close 

Making it work in real time

As nurses became more familiar with administering lenacapavir, the clinics also refined how they moved patients through the service, from the initial consultation to receiving the injection.

Patients first met a navigator who explained the available services. After registration, an HIV test and a check of their vital signs, they saw the research nurse.

The clinics later began using the waiting time more effectively, with navigators introducing patients to PrEP and other services before their consultations.

Initially, appointments could take about an hour and a half. As the clinics refined their workflow and nurses became more familiar with the process, Senokwane says visits took about an hour or less.

"Training manuals and guidelines provide all the theoretical knowledge and framework for delivering lenacapavir," Martin explains.

"But, that real-world experience gives you a little bit more insight into things that you can only learn by working with clients."

Each one teach one

Senokwane's experience eventually helped her become a mentor to other nurses.

"The mentorship was really very important. We've got support from our pharmacist, and then we've got support from our sub-investigator at site. So everyone needs to be mentored until you are really 100% sure that you can do it on your own," she says.

When non-research nurses started providing lenacapavir in June at the study sites, she went there to demonstrate the technique. Some nurses she had trained also helped their colleagues.

"They were always grateful that we really helped them. So they really appreciated it. The more you practice, the better you become," says Senokwane.

Lessons from the clinics also informed training. Videos demonstrating how to prepare and administer lenacapavir were produced by Wits RHI, alongside webinars. Martin says the videos would be incorporated into future training.

"It's always helpful to see something in practice. With a new product, although it can be explained theoretically, it is helpful to actually see a provider and a client interaction," she says.

World.title: Malawi: Schools Urged to Adapt As Heatwave Warning Issued Across Malawi
World.content:
Schools and other learning institutions have been urged to implement immediate measures to protect learners and staff following a heatwave alert issued by the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS).

The Department has forecast temperatures of up to 42C in parts of the Southern Region, with unusually high temperatures also expected across the Central, Northern and lakeshore areas.

In a statement, Secretary for Education Dr Ken Ndala said institutions should strictly adhere to precautionary measures aimed at safeguarding learners, teachers and support staff while maintaining continuity in education.

Schools have been advised to adjust timetables, relax uniform requirements and adopt flexible learning arrangements where necessary to reduce exposure to extreme heat.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The ministry has also directed institutions to suspend or reschedule outdoor activities, including sports, assemblies, parades and manual work, during the hottest part of the day, between 10am and 3pm.

Additional guidance includes ensuring continuous access to safe drinking water, encouraging regular hydration, keeping classrooms cool and well-ventilated, making use of shaded areas and avoiding overcrowding.

Schools have also been asked to pay particular attention to vulnerable groups, including young children, people with albinism, pregnant members of staff and those living with chronic health conditions.

"The ministry also reminds institutions to make use of the El Niño Practical Guidance for the Education Sector 2026-2027 booklets that have been distributed to strengthen preparedness and response to climate-related hazards," the statement said.

The advisory forms part of wider efforts to minimise the impact of extreme weather conditions on learning and to reduce health risks associated with prolonged exposure to high temperatures.

World.title: Senegal: General Strike Continues Amid Protests Against New Labour Laws
World.content:
Dakar — Senegal's labour unions have called for a 72-hour general strike, from October 21 to 23, 2026. The government disputes the legality of the strike, saying the notice filed by the unions doesn't comply with the procedures. This standoff comes amid ongoing tensions surrounding the reform of the Labor Code and the Social Security Code.

The confrontation between the government and the trade unions has entered a new phase. At the call of the Trade Union Front for the Defense of Labor (FSDT) and the mobilized trade union federations, workers are invited to observe three days of strike action to protest, in particular, against the conditions under which the new labor and social protection laws were adopted.

For several months, unions have been denouncing a process they deem insufficiently consultative. On July 10, the FSDT had already announced a general strike to express its opposition to the approach taken by the authorities. Despite this protest, the two texts were promulgated on September 3, 2026, under laws no. 2026-18 and no. 2026-19, before their publication in the Official Journal on September 18th.

A disagreement over the legality of the movement



Faced with this new call for mobilization, the Ministry of Public Service, Labor, and Public Service Reform considers the strike order unlawful. According to information reported by PressAfrik, the administration contests the use of a single strike notice to cover the public, semi-public, and private sectors, which are subject to separate procedures.

In the private and semi-public sectors, the Labor Code stipulates that the dispute must be notified to the Labor and Social Security Inspector or the relevant Director General, as applicable. If no agreement is reached, or in the event of partial conciliation, a thirty-day notice period may then be given to the company's management.

For civil servants, the ministry reminds them that written notice must specify the reasons for and duration of the strike, with one month's notice given before the action begins. Local government employees, for their part, must notify the president of the departmental council or the mayor concerned of their strike notice.

The administration warns that failure to comply with these formalities may result in salary deductions for days not worked and disciplinary action. It also mentions potential consequences for the right to compensation and damages in the event of termination of the employment contract.

For more, read the original story in French.

World.title: Sudan: Drone Strikes Killed At Least 306 People in Three Weeks
World.content:
UN human rights chief Volker Türk on Friday strongly condemned an escalation in drone strikes across Sudan this month, which killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October alone.

The strikes, attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), hit homes, markets, hospitals, displacement sites, power stations and water sources in Kordofan, Darfur, Blue Nile, Khartoum and other states, according to the UN human rights office (OHCHR).

"The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll," Mr. Türk said.

Targeted by both sides

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In a particularly disturbing trend, the office documented numerous strikes on displacement sites, where people who had already fled the fighting had sought shelter.

Between 6 and 10 October, alleged drone strikes attributed to military government forces on shelters for displaced people in Ghubeish and El Nuhud in West Kordofan killed at least 25 civilians, including women and children.

On 9 October, an alleged RSF drone struck a crowd of displaced people engaged in artisanal gold mining near a displacement site in Abu Shendi, Blue Nile, killing at least 31 people, most of them women and children.

On 18 October, at least 139 people were killed when a transportation truck was hit in a "double tap" repeat strike in Dibab, West Kordofan, an area controlled by the RSF militia.

Markets and hospitals have also been hit, including an RSF-attributed strike on Um Darfa hospital in Blue Nile on 11 October that seriously injured two health workers and left the facility non-operational.

"Scores of civilians have been killed, including internally displaced persons, and vital infrastructure and services have been eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis," said OHCHR Spokesperson Seif Magango.

Deadly strike

Peacekeepers with the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) this week visited communities affected by a drone attack on 19 October on Amiet Market and the Todach area in Abyei, the disputed oil-rich region between Sudan and South Sudan. The attack killed more than 80 people.

Close 

UNISFA troops were the first to reach the scene, where "every shop was burning", said Lieutenant Colonel Muhammad Farooq, commander of the Mission's Pakistani battalion.

The Mission deployed quick reaction and firefighting teams to stop the fire spreading and took more than 27 injured people to its hospital in Todach, according to Acting Force Commander Brigadier General Adebowale Ajabge.

Angelina Musa Diaw, a trader and mother of three, said she had lost everything. "No work, everything is gone," she said. "I am here with my children. But I need help."

Call for ceasefire

Mr. Türk called on the parties to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law (IHL), including by not directing attacks against civilians and civilian objects.

"Broader peace efforts must squarely address the continued influx of arms that is fuelling the conflict and press for an end to the transfer of arms that are used in manifest disregard of the IHL obligations protecting civilians," he said.

"I urge both parties to the conflict, and their affiliates, to commit to a ceasefire," the High Commissioner added, stressing that a negotiated settlement with human rights at its core, underpinned by accountability, is the only feasible pathway to sustainable peace in Sudan.

World.title: Brandi Glanville says doctors are 'taking my face off' in exploratory surgery after years of health issues

Brandi Glanville is taking a major step in her ongoing health battle by going under the knife.

During an episode of her "Brandi Glanville Unfiltered" podcast, shared on Thursday, Oct. 22, the 53-year-old reality star went into detail about the "exploratory surgery" she is scheduled to have on Friday.

"Dr. Carlo Honrado is taking my face off on Friday and going to do an exploratory surgery to kind of do a power wash under my skin," she said. "And then he knows where there's two definite spots, like either fungal balls or something alive. I think it's alive personally cause it moves when it wants."

She explained that after four years of dealing with the issue, she is "super excited" but also "scared to death" because she has "never had facial surgery" and has heard the procedure is "more intensive than a facelift."

FORMER REALITY STAR OPENS UP ABOUT NEW DIAGNOSIS AFTER YEARS-LONG HEALTH ORDEAL

While she is nervous, Glanville is hopeful the surgery will be a success, as facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon, Dr. Honrado, "comes highly recommended." She noted that she is "okay" with the $5,000 price tag, telling herself, "what if he actually does take it out and it's done?"

"It started in my face, my cheek and my jawbone, and then it went over my head back in my neck. Now it's down my spine," she explained.

She went on to say that the doctor told her if he is able to "cut that head off the beast", getting rid of the rest of it will be more manageable.

Glanville previously shared that she believed she picked up a parasite after visiting Morocco in 2023. She suffered from facial paralysis and was initially diagnosed with stress-induced angioedema.

World.content:
New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo is known for being a bit of a loose cannon on the football field.

He runs hard and crashes into defenders left and right. On Sunday, NFL officials suggested he crossed a line while trying to truck over a Houston Texans player.

Skattebo took a handoff from quarterback J.J. McCarthy in the first quarter. Skattebo found a crease, lowered his helmet and ran over an opposing defender. The running back put his head down and collided with safety M.J. Stewart.

A flag was thrown on the play and Skattebo was called for unnecessary roughness because he lowered his helmet.

It’s really unclear what Skattebo was supposed to do in that situation. Helmet-to-helmet crashes happen in the NFL and usually a flag is thrown if the player on the receiving end of the damage is considered to be a defenseless player or a defender leads with their helmet when making a tackle – not the opposite. Even Giants head coach John Harbaugh seemed perplexed.

The Giants and Texans were in a tight matchup in Week 7. The two teams were tied going into the half 14-14.

Skattebo had come under the microscope because he had no carries against the New Orleans Saints in Week 6. The Giants appeared to make some kind of point with Skattebo’s inaction. Harbaugh insisted last week he didn’t bench Skattebo.

"It wasn’t by design for him not to carry the ball," Harbaugh said. "Just when he was in there, we didn’t call any runs. You’re not thinking about which back is in the game and how many runs they’re getting. It’s we were going to give them all an equal shot, give them a chance, see who got a hot hand maybe, see who could get going with it. We weren’t planning on being down by 24, that’s for sure."

World.title: Firehouse Subs co-founder dies after building beloved American sandwich chain with brother
World.content:

Chris Sorensen, a co-founder of the sandwich chain Firehouse Subs, has died at 65.

Before entering the restaurant industry, Sorensen was a professional guitarist, even sitting in with bands including Huey Lewis and the News, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Foreigner and Earth, Wind & Fire, according to his obituary.

He went on to become a firefighter, following in the footsteps of his father, Robert.

EVERY BITE COUNTS AS SANDWICH SHOP DITCHES TRADITIONAL SUB-BUILDING METHOD

After working at the Brevard County Fire Department and the Jacksonville International Airport Fire and Rescue Department, Chris spent 10 years as an engineer and EMT at the Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department, where his dad also worked at the time.

In 1994, Chris and his younger brother, Robin, co-founded Firehouse Subs, opening the first location in their hometown of Jacksonville.

They had less than $100 in their checking accounts at the time, according to Nation’s Restaurant News.

CLICK HERE TO 

Surprisingly, the first-ever order at the chain’s flagship location was not a sub, but two hot dogs with everything on them, which consisted of about 10 ingredients, Robin Sorensen told the Jacksonville Daily Record in 2020.

"We were so focused on the subs, we weren’t prepared for that order. Needless to say, it was a long ticket time," he said.

Featuring steamed meats and cheeses piled high on warm toasted rolls, Firehouse sandwiches soon became a hit.

Chris took creative ownership of the interior of Firehouse Subs restaurants, outfitting each location with a custom mural depicting fire and police service unique to the restaurant’s town.

A collector of historical artifacts, he ensured that the legacy of Firehouse Subs was preserved, serving as the chain's unofficial archivist.

After being sold in 2021 for one billion dollars to Restaurant Brands International, which also owns Burger King, the Firehouse Subs fleet grew to more than 1,200 locations.

In 2005, Chris and Robin Sorensen created the Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation, with a mission of providing first-responders with life-saving equipment, tools and education.

World.title: Country star Cody Johnson says Nashville wanted to change him before success
World.content:

Nashville wanted Cody Johnson to ditch his cowboy hat before giving him a shot at country music stardom.

The Texas-born country star said he walked away from a record deal after executives suggested he swap his signature cowboy look for a baseball cap — a move he viewed as a demand to change who he was before he could make it in the music business.

"They wanted a baseball cap, which I have nothing against, but it was the approach. It was the 'you're great, but once we change you, you'll make it.' And it pissed me off," he said in an interview with "CBS Mornings." "I tipped my hat and said, 'Thank you for your time.'"

CARRIE UNDERWOOD SAYS HER FAMILY COULD BE 'SELF-SUSTAINED' ON TENNESSEE FARM AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD SPOTLIGHT

It was a gamble that could have cost him his shot at stardom.

Instead, Johnson spent the next 10 years building a career on his own terms, playing bars and honky-tonks before becoming one of country music's biggest stars.

During his interview, Johnson spoke candidly about his rise to fame and the years of work behind his success.

COUNTRY SINGER CODY JOHNSON FORCED TO STOP 'GOD BLESS AMERICA' PERFORMANCE AS VIOLENT BRAWL BREAKS OUT

Long before arena crowds and industry recognition, the singer was a small-town Texas kid who dreamed of becoming a rodeo star.

He eventually traded bull riding for music after years of injuries and setbacks and selling CDs in rodeo parking lots as he tried to build a following.

The country star also struggled to believe his ambitions were within reach.

"Truthfully, in my core, I didn't feel I was capable of attaining a goal that big, you know, to be a huge country music star, to own a cattle ranch," Johnson said.

After turning down the label opportunity, he spent years playing small venues, struggling financially and spending long stretches away from his family to keep his career alive.

World.content:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are scoring points in the most unorthodox ways against the Carolina Panthers on Sunday.

The Bucs led the Panthers convincingly with a 33-6 lead at halftime and 8 of their points came in freakish fashion.

The freakish fashion?

A defensive two-point conversion by cornerback Zyon McCullom.

A big-man touchdown fumble return by 280-pound defensive tackle Calijah Kancey.

Not typical.

BAKER MAYFIELD LEAVES GAME AFTER WRITHING IN PAIN ON TURF IN TAMPA BAY WHEN THUMB ON THROWING HAND INJURED

Let's begin with the Kancey score first. The Bucs have so far smothered the Panthers' offense and evidence of that was Al-Quadin Muhammad's strip-sack of Carolina quarterback Bryce Young.

Well, if you got a strip, you've got a loose football and Kancey scooped up the loose ball on a bounce, outran an offensive lineman 32 yards to the end zone and completed the score by performing a flip over the goal line.

None of that is typical big man behavior.

BAKER MAYFIELD LOSES BET TO COACH TODD BOWLES, HAS 'ROUGH COUPLE OF DAYS' INCLUDING AT PRESS CONFERENCE

This is dream-of-a-lifetime stuff for any defensive player. It's practically unheard of for a defensive lineman.

And, interestingly, Kancey's rare moment was not the most unorthodox of this game for the Bucs.

We present McCollum's two-pointer.

The Panthers had cut the deficit with a 50-yard hookup between Young and tight end Darren Waller. That cut Tampa Bay's lead to 17-6.

But on the ensuing extra point, McCullom snatched a blocked extra point out of the air and returned it for, well, a conversion for the Bucs.

Two points.

Zany.

McCollum, by the way, is having a day. He also intercepted Young later in the first half.

The Bucs are in last place in the NFC South with a 1-5 record. But Baker Mayfield started this game after missing the previous three games with a dislocated thumb on his right (throwing) hand.

Mayfield threw a touchdown pass to Tez Johnson to give the Bucs a 33-6 halftime lead. Tampa Bay's 33 first-half points is the third-most in franchise history and most since 2021.

World.title: Parker McCollum wants his sons to learn the lesson hunting and ranch life taught him growing up
World.content:
Parker McCollum has come a long way from the little boy who couldn't wait to tag along on hunting trips with his dad. Now, with two sons of his own, the country music star is looking forward to being on the other side of those childhood memories.

And he's already getting a head start.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

McCollum, who welcomed his second son with wife Hallie Ray in July, recently spent several days at the family ranch with his oldest boy, 2-year-old Major.

"I was taking him with me to kind of, you know, just do some ranch stuff," McCollum told OutKick OutDoors in an exclusive interview. "He can't really. He just kind of stands out there and pulls grass out of the ground while I'm working or whatever."

Major might not be much help around the ranch just yet, but McCollum certainly doesn't mind. After all, he remembers exactly what it was like to be that little boy.

Watch Parker McCollum's whole interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

"I remember those days so vividly," he said. "My dad would get me out of school early on a Friday to go down to the lease or the ranch or whatever, and we would let it rip all weekend. And a lot of times it was just him and I.

"To say that I look forward to doing that for him and with him is an understatement."

A lifelong love of hunting

Hunting has been part of McCollum's life for as long as he can remember.

In a 2022 interview with NRA Country, the Texas native recalled going bird hunting with his father when he was around 8 years old, carrying a single-shot .410 shotgun. He also identified his dad as one of his favorite hunting buddies.

But McCollum's love for the outdoors started even before he was old enough to participate.

During a 2024 interview with Audacy, McCollum remembered crying when his father and other family members left for hunting trips without him because he was too young to come along.

Once he finally got his chance, he was hooked.

CHARTER CAPTAIN JONATHAN MOSS EXPLAINS HOW TO GET KIDS HOOKED ON FISHING FROM AN EARLY AGE

That outdoors-centered upbringing extended beyond hunting season, too. McCollum spent summers working cattle, branding steers and tending to his grandfather's ranch alongside his cousins.

Now he's hoping Major and his younger brother, Rocker, will grow up with that same appreciation for the outdoors.

And for McCollum, it's about much more than harvesting deer.

'So good for your soul'

With a demanding music career, two young children and a schedule that often keeps him on the road, McCollum understands how difficult it can be to slow down.

That's exactly why he believes time outdoors is so important.

"There is nothing I love more than sitting in a tree in East Texas or South Texas or the Midwest. Even if you don’t see a dadgum deer," he told OutKick OutDoors. "There's just something about it that's so good for your soul."

McCollum explained that his family's trips to the ranch aren’t about checking things off a to-do list or packing as much activity into the day as possible.

"Our whole intention was just slowing it down and turning it off and just spending time as a family, and no agenda," he said. "We wake up late and cook breakfast, and hunt in the evenings, and crockpot dinner, and ride around."

It's a deliberate departure from the pace of everyday life — one McCollum says is becoming increasingly difficult to escape.

And that's precisely the lesson he hopes his sons will carry into adulthood.

"Don't ever get so busy or worried about other stuff that you forget to do this."



We couldn’t have said it better ourselves.

World.title: Mary Peltola delays campaign events after sustaining ‘minor injuries’ in car crash
World.content:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola is rescheduling several upcoming campaign events after she and her family sustained “minor” injuries in a car crash, her campaign announced on Sunday.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement.

“Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families,” Bruce added.

Peltola was en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives’ annual banquet on Saturday when a vehicle transporting the candidate and her family was struck by another driver, according to the campaign.

The police department in Anchorage confirmed Sunday that a collision involving three vehicles occurred on Saturday evening and those involved sustained “non-life threatening injuries.”

Police added that the incident is under investigation.

Peltola, a Democrat, is locked in a competitive Senate race against GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. She was elected to the House in 2022 but narrowly lost her re-election bid in 2024, the same year that President Donald Trump won the state by 13 percentage points.

Sullivan’s re-election race, in which he’s seeking a third term, is tighter than expected, with Alaska voters tying Trump to high gas and grocery prices resulting from the ongoing war with Iran.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance rallied voters in Alaska separately earlier this month.

Republicans have accused Democrats of recruiting another candidate named Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate, saying that voters may be confused by the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot if they plan to vote for the incumbent senator.

Democrats have not taken credit for recruiting the second Dan Sullivan into the race. He’ll appear on the ballot as Dan J. Sullivan, while the incumbent senator will be identified by his name, political party and a clear notation that he’s the incumbent.

Last week, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against Alaska’s election officials, seeking to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. They cited Dan J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot as a point of “voter confusion.”

On Saturday, Democrats filed a motion urging a federal judge to dismiss the case.
