LISTEN | Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the province's path forward: Calgary Eyeopener 13:16 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the province's path forward We're still learning about how Albertans are responding to nine of the province's referendum questions. As a picture begins to emerge, Alberta Premier, Danielle Smith, joined us to discuss how her government will act upon the results.

All 5 immigration questions pass

The five questions concerning immigration included proposals for the province taking more control over immigration from Ottawa, requiring residents to have an “Alberta-approved immigration status” to be eligible for public and social services, and showing proof of citizenship before voting in elections.

If all five of the successful proposals become law, Alberta could require some temporary residents — such as international students or temporary foreign workers — to have lived in the province for at least 12 months before they can qualify for some provincial social supports such as childcare subsidies, and charge a “reasonable fee or premium” for their use of the public health care and education systems.

Smith has floated the idea of charging temporary residents a $1,900 fee for access to public health care, akin to a premium charged by the United Kingdom.

WATCH | Alberta's referendum questions on immigration, explained: Alberta's referendum questions on immigration, explained | Duration closed caption 14:53 There are five referendum questions for Albertans to consider on immigration. CBC's Rukhsar Ali breaks down each one to look at what happens if you vote 'yes' or 'no.'

Calgarian Camille Katigbak, who owns the marketing agency Katigbak Technologies, is one of the more than half of voters who supported immigration changes. She is also the daughter of immigrants from the Philippines.

To her, the proposed changes make sense. She worries about too many people putting pressure on the system.

“I think if we just limit and kind of pre-qualify, we make sure okay, these people are here for the right reasons, I think that would really help our system be more streamlined and we're not overwhelmed,” she said.

“I do know that we have to help our neighbours too. Like we have to think about helping others, but at what cost, right?”

The question about requiring proof of Canadian citizenship to vote in provincial elections was also something she supported.

WATCH | Why Alberta's fight with Ottawa over immigration won't end soon: Why Alberta's fight with Ottawa over immigration won't end soon | Duration closed caption 3:21 Albertans may have overwhelmingly rejected separating from Canada, but referendum results show significant support for more provincial control over immigration. CBC's Lyndsay Duncombe examines what that means for relations with Ottawa, and the concerns it raises for newcomers in the province.

But not everyone feels as positively about the results as Katigbak does.

Calgarian Dozie Anyaegbunam, who came to Canada from Nigeria in 2021, has been critical of the referendum and had hoped the immigration questions would fail.

While they did pass, the host of The Newcomers podcast said he’s encouraged by how many people voted against them.

“I think it's good to kind of see that it is not an overwhelming majority,” he said. “Even if the government says they have a mandate, they don't have a full mandate. And that gives me some hope in terms of how we move forward from here as a community.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Tuesday that he and Smith had discussed "other priorities" facing Canadians, namely, immigration.

"Constitutional change is difficult, it's long," Carney said. "I believe, for example, on the issue of immigration and co-operation between the federal government and the provinces for sustainable immigration … that we can accomplish that without constitutional change."

Voters reject all 4 constitutional questions

All four Constitution-related questions were rejected, including the proposals relating to the province selecting its own judges for certain courts, abolishing the federal Senate , opting out of some federal programs , and prioritizing provincial laws over federal laws in some areas where they conflict.

Gerard Kennedy, University of Alberta constitutional law professor, said getting the public interested in constitutional amendment has never been easy, and this referendum has not proved to be an exception.

But on the matter of selecting judges, Smith isn’t the only premier who has shown interest in a constitutional change.

Saskatchewan, Quebec and Ontario also have an appetite for selecting their own judges, but Kennedy said the odds of a constitutional amendment “I would think are very, very low.”

“What we could have is agreements from the federal government to change the system to give the provinces more of a weight, but it will ultimately be the decision of the federal government to decide whom to appoint.”

Campaigning less noticeable on the other 9 questions

Amongst third-party advertisers, campaigning on the nine non-separation questions was noticeably less prominent in much of the referendum conversation.

Perhaps the most notable, “No to the Nine” became a memorable slogan on the federalist side, based on signs erected by longtime political strategist Stephen Carter’s campaign Alberta’s Voice.

As early results came in, Carter said he still considered his campaign a success, though the five immigration questions being passed was “a significant blow.”

“Immigrants come to Alberta to do two things: create jobs and do jobs,” he said. “They don't come to take advantage of our healthcare system, they don't come to take advantage of our education system.”

On the flipside, the separatist group Alberta Prosperity Project recently encouraged supporters to “decline” marking an answer on the other nine questions, writing on social media it “would not lend its name to bogus referendum questions.”

A lesser-known group called Alberta Women for Independence was one of the few organizations whose blue pro-separation signs also encouraged yes votes for the nine questions.

When could changes happen?

On Friday, the United Conservative Party laid out its plans for legislation in the upcoming fall sitting, but said Albertans shouldn’t expect to see new laws tied to how they voted in the referendum.

When it comes to new immigration policies, Evan Menzies, vice president at Crestview Strategy, suspects some policies, like requiring non-permanent residents to pay for social services, could take longer to implement.

“That could be too disruptive too fast, there might need to be some sort of transition phase,” said Menzies, who was also formerly a political staffer with the UCP.

“And especially considering that there’s an election 12 months away, I don’t know how much the province has an appetite to push too hard too fast with that respect.”

World.title: Sgt. Morgan Wong of CFB Wainwright remembered as loyal friend, dedicated soldier at funeral
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A funeral home in central Edmonton was full Sunday morning, with most in attendance wearing poppies over their hearts to honour the sergeant who died last weekend at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, in central Alberta.

Eight service members carried the casket of Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, draped in the Maple Leaf, to the front of the room as bagpipes played him in.

The flag was later replaced with a yellow descendants’ blanket — a traditional Chinese textile used during funerals — before a shrine, featuring a framed photo of Wong, fruit, rice and flowers, was placed in front of the casket and other Buddhist funeral customs were performed.

“Each one of us has our own special memories of Morgan, and I hope holding onto those memories will remind us to live our lives with courage and integrity, like he did,” his sister, Megan, said in a speech during the service.

“He was too young when he left us,” she said. “But I hope his life will be a reminder for each of us to use the time we have to achieve a life we would be proud of.”

Megan described her brother as brave, warm and hilarious, a loyal friend and dedicated soldier. She added that Wong was close to their mother — and that now they’re together again.

The family also offered their condolences to the other soldiers who died and were injured at CFB Wainwright.

A fire at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17, resulting from a training exercise, was first reported in the base's grenade launcher range — a "permanent danger area" that base firefighters couldn't enter. Strong winds in the region that day spread the flames quickly, overwhelming service members and eventually burning beyond the base.

The fire caused dozens of casualties and killed four service members including Wong, a member from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment who served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“The love that Canadians have shown for Sgt. Wong means more to all of us than we could ever explain. We will always remember him, and his family will forever be part of our family,” Lt.-Col. Bryn Wright, commanding officer of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, said in a written statement to journalists Sunday.

In a statement issued earlier this week, Wong's family expressed their love for him and how proud he had made them. They said he joined the military in 2017 and was training at CFB Wainwright last weekend to prepare for a second deployment to Europe.

During Sunday's service, Wright, who knew Wong throughout the sergeant's military career, shared three stories that spoke to Wong's dedication to service and discipline to hold trainees to the highest standard.

"Passionate, professional, committed to excellence — that was Sgt. Morgan Wong," he said, later adding that every service member in attendance Sunday will carry his example with them.

Some fellow service members and Wong’s longtime friends also shared stories during the ceremony that highlighted similar traits: humour, integrity, generosity and a willingness to help out however he could. Each expressed gratitude for knowing him.

Since the news of his death, friends and people Wong volunteered with described him as a passionate volunteer and a mentor.

World.title: Who is B.C.'s new premier Lorne Doerkson?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson struck political gold Saturday night.

The former small-town newspaper publisher delivered a stunning defeat to David Eby's NDP and led the B.C. Conservatives to a commanding majority government.

Early Sunday morning, Doerkson's Conservatives were leading in 64 ridings, reducing the NDP to just 27 seats and toppling several cabinet ministers.

It's a remarkable turnaround for a political party that was in disarray just five weeks ago, days before a snap election was called.

But where his political opponents may have seen weakness, Doerkson said British Columbians chose instead to seize an opportunity.

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," Doerkson told a throng of more than 1,000 supporters at the Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver.

"But tonight the whole map counts."

WATCH | Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gives victory speech: FULL SPEECH: Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson's victory speech | Duration closed caption 17:01

Rodeos to newspapers to politics

Born in New Westminster, Doerkson grew up in Surrey and the B.C. Interior, before settling in Williams Lake, where he raised a family.

He spent 20 years publishing community newspapers and volunteering with local business and community service groups before entering politics.

"That was a very good education for me," he told supporters. "You learn what’s really going on in a town: who’s hiring, who’s closing, who’s hoping."

Doerkson was first elected in Cariboo-Chilcotin as a B.C. Liberal in 2020, and later joined John Rustad's fledgling Conservative caucus.

His victory makes him the first premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett left office in 1986.

Doerkson was on his way home from South Africa last month when he learned his Conservative caucus colleagues wanted him to take over the party as interim leader.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay had just resigned after months of scandals that led to the departure or expulsion of more than a dozen MLAs.

Doerkson admitted he needed convincing.

"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," he said in a pre-election interview with CBC News.

Lorne Doerkson speaks to supporters in the crowd during provincial election night Saturday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Promises to cut income taxes, red tape

Doerkson spent his victory speech Saturday night introducing himself to British Columbians at the same time as celebrating the "trailblazers" who came to the province searching for gold and a better life.

It's a spirit he told supporters that still animates the province, where people want to build something big, from resource communities through to the big metro areas.

"That is the trailblazing spirit of British Columbia and it never left, it just needs government that’s on its side," he said.

WATCH | CBC News projects a Conservative government: CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government | Duration closed caption 1:59

Doerkson reiterated promises to cut red tape "like it’s never been cut before," speed up forestry and mining permits, and triple natural gas production by 2035.

"A province only works if all of it works," he said.

"A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps the port busy in Delta. It’s one economy and it runs through every town on our map."

Doerkson also pledged no new taxes and health care that is "fully and publicly funded."

Still, questions remain about how he'll pay for everything, including a promise to cut income taxes by $1,000 a year.

The province is already on track to see a $13.8-billion deficit in 2026-27.

The NDP spent their campaign warning that the Conservatives' platform could mean cuts to health care and education.

Speaking in Vancouver Saturday, Doerkson reiterated election promises, including to cut red tape 'like it’s never been cut before.' (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Overcoming divisions

As premier-designate, Doerkson now faces the challenge of not only governing but keeping together a coalition that includes social conservatives and more centrist, fiscal conservatives.

And though he has promised to repeal B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People’s Act, he appealed to First Nations communities as partners in the province’s development.

"This future is one we build together as partners with the certainty that all of us need," he said.

One source of division Doerkson won't need to deal with immediately will be the NDP.

With preliminary results showing New Democrats reduced to fewer than 30 seats, the Official Opposition's first priority will be choosing a new leader to replace David Eby who announced Saturday that he will step down.

World.title: Is this Quebec-developed fruit the 'apple of the future'?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Orléans apple — developed on Île d’Orléans, Que. — is hitting grocery store shelves this fall, but has been in the works for nearly 25 years.

Beginning back in 2002, producers handpicked pollen from Honeycrisps and Empire apple flowers, and then spent years crossbreeding them until they arrived at the bright red and crisp Orléans. While it has been available in Quebec orchards for about two years, it's only now hitting grocery store shelves.

"I have some clients coming here asking especially for that kind," says Karen Morin. She thinks it just might be "the apple of the future."

The co-owner of the Verger du Roy in Portneuf grows 57 different types of apples, but Morin says the Orléans is growing more and more popular this year with apple pickers.

"It's a mix of Honeycrisp and Empire, so these two together, it's like a bomb. It's really, really good, so sweet [and] still really crispy," says Morin. "In the future, our children, it won't be the Honeycrisp anymore that will be the top one, it will be the Orléans."

Morin says that, while apple preferences can vary from generation to generation, people are always looking for apples that stay crisper longer. She believes that's why the Orléans apple is increasing in popularity.

Karen Morin says the Orléans apple has been growing in popularity for the past two years with apple pickers, but many people still aren't aware of the latest apple varieties coming to the market. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

"It's like on the top of the list for firmness, and it's almost top of the list for sugar content," says

Benoit Caron, the owner of La Maison de la Pomme. Caron planted 20,000 Orléans trees at his orchard in Frelighsburg about five years ago.

"It's not the first apple created in Quebec, but it's the first one that we can supply at least 10 months a year because of [its] conservation," says Caron.

He adds that this particular variety is great as a snack, "but it's also a really good apple for cooking. It will hold itself together. So if you do apple custard or apple pie, you will have the nice apple slice that will stay together."

More supply and more demand for Quebec produce

Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle, the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, says it's good to have new varieties to appeal to all the different types of consumers, but that the demand for Quebec produce has also been growing recently.

"If these new varieties can help us gain market shares from imported apples and that we can source more of Quebec-grown apples to consumers, it's a win for everyone," he says.

Brunelle says recent tensions with the U.S. and tariff woes did have an impact. "Consumers had more of an interest in locally sourced food," he says, and apples were no exception.

There’s been a bigger interest for locally sourced apples for the past two years, "and it doesn't seem to be slowing down," says the executive director of the Producteurs de pommes du Québec, Jérôme-Antoine Brunelle. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

"That interest for locally sourced fruit helps us out, and we see that Quebec consumers are more conscientious of where their food comes from," says Brunelle.

He says he is aware, however, that producers and grocery stores must make sure Quebec apples are clearly identified as such in produce aisles to attract more consumers .

Different regions, different apples, different ciders

Claude Jolicoeur, an author who's published three books about apples and cider production, wants to increase the number of apple varieties in Quebec, specifically for cider. "And eventually maybe to have an appellation ‘regional cider,'" he says.

Jolicoeur says this could bring Quebec cider production to another level, similar to wine production in Italy — where different grape varieties, grown in different regions, produce different types of wines, with distinct flavours.

Morin, for instance, says Quebec-grown apples can also taste like other fruits, such as bananas, pineapples, strawberries, and even chestnuts.

"You can compare apples with apples, but they're different," she says.

Regardless of their provenance or flavour, cider apples would not be the same ones as those picked in orchards, or bought at the grocery store, however. "When you want to sell apples in a grocery store, that apple has to be beautiful," says Jolicoeur.

In the cider context, however, he notes, "no one is going to see the apple, so what it looks like is not important at all."

Jolicoeur hopes Quebec cider and apple producers will grow more and more Quebec apple varieties in the coming years.

However, apple producers reiterate, in the meantime, several apple varieties are already available year round, not only in the fall — including the brand new Orléans.

World.title: Ukraine says its military did not violate Starlink terms, disputing Elon Musk claim
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian officials have disputed claims by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that the country's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone strikes.

Serhii Beskrestnov, a defence technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said long-standing restrictions on the civilian system in Ukraine made such offensive use impossible.

"It's very strange that Elon Musk doesn't know about the restrictions on Starlink's operation in Ukraine," he wrote in an online post.

SpaceX's Starlink and its military-focused Starshield service are critical to Ukraine's wartime connectivity. Earlier this month, Ukrainian drones connected to Starshield lost connectivity at high speeds, disrupting air defences during daily Russian air attacks. Officials said the so-called speed caps were lifted on Saturday, and the service was restored.

Still, questions have persisted about who ordered the interruptions to satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks .

Writing on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that drones operated via the civilian Starlink system had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h within Ukraine and did not work in Russia.

Serhii Beskrestnov, also known as Flash, an adviser to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says it would not be possible for Ukraine's military to use Starlink for offensive drone strikes. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes," he said.

Musk acknowledged on Saturday that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication.

U.S. President Donald Trump has maintained that he didn't make that call, while Vice-President JD Vance has hinted at White House co-ordination with Musk.

Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

They also added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Trump's reported deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia that Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

New push to end the war

The restoration of Starlink service followed a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month.

On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by efforts from both first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors.

He said the attacks — many of them deadly — had affected nine regions of the country, damaging power plants, grain stores, civilian homes and commercial facilities.

WATCH | Mark Carney on consequences of Starlink slowdown: Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine | Duration closed caption 3:10 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is concerned about the reported slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, which created 'real consequences.' He says Canadians likewise 'do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view' and compromise Canadian sovereignty.

More civilian deaths

Russia launched more than 20 attacks on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region overnight into Sunday, using drones and an aerial bomb, according to local authorities. Three people died at the scene and a fourth man later died in hospital, regional military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha reported, while over a dozen people were injured.

In Vinnytsia, a city in central Ukraine, at least six people were injured when a Russian drone struck a residential building, according to the state emergency service. The attack also damaged a nearby care home, with emergency crews evacuating 15 elderly residents, the service said.

Also according to the emergency service, consecutive Russian strikes on a shopping centre in Kharkiv injured four people late on Saturday, including three rescue workers. Ukraine has long accused Russia of so-called double-tap strikes, in which an initial attack is followed by another once rescuers arrive on the scene.

Firefighters work at the site of the shopping mall missile strike in Kharkiv on Saturday. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)

Russia's Defence Ministry on Sunday claimed its forces targeted multiple sites in and around Kharkiv, including a shopping and logistics centre that it said had stored dual-use goods meant for the Ukrainian military.

In Russia, two people were killed and 13 others injured in Belgorod, a city 40 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, following "mass" nighttime drone strikes by Kyiv, regional Gov. Alexander Shuvayev reported on Sunday.

In the Russian city of Oryol, body of a fourth victim was pulled from the rubble the day after a Ukrainian strike on an industrial plant, local Gov. Andrey Klychkov reported. On Saturday, local authorities said three people had been killed in the attack.

Ukraine's general staff that day said its forces hit an electronics plant in Oryol that makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.

World.title: There’s disappointment and hope among Albertans who supported the idea of independence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Throughout the referendum campaign, CBC News used First Person writing, community focus groups and small engagement pop-ups to understand why Albertans were planning to vote the way they were.

We met many people on both sides of the debate.

Now that the results have come in, with three-quarters of Albertans voting to stay in Canada, we reached out to some of the community members who supported the other side to see how they feel and what they would like to see happen next.

There were many emotions — hope, disappointment, contentment.

Vicky Bayford lives in Innisfail, Alta., north of Calgary. She's pictured here in her backyard in 2026. (Submitted by Vicky Bayford)

‘This isn’t a hidden conversation anymore’

Vicky Bayford saw the results when she finished scrutineering early Tuesday morning. She had been hopeful, watching numbers near 50 per cent for Option 2 from her polling station in Innisfail, a town of nearly 9,000 people an hour’s drive north of Calgary.

Bayford said the provincewide tally of 25 per cent was disappointing, but not surprising.

“I’ve always known this was going to be an uphill battle.”

Bayford works in oil and gas, and has been heavily involved with separatism since 2020. She believes Option 2 lost because many conservatives decided to give Premier Danielle Smith a chance to make changes within Canada.

But Bayford also believes the last 18 months of work have been a boon to the independence movement, despite the loss.

“This isn’t a hidden conversation anymore like it was when I got involved in 2020,” she said. “Now at least it’s on the radar.”

Friendships were formed as supporters signed petitions and attended town halls. Pro-independence organizations will make sure that social aspect doesn’t go away, she said.

But there is something she does hope will change. Bayford wrote a First Person piece for CBC News during the campaign, and then sat down to discuss it with three other First Person authors on CBC's West of Centre .

One of the authors, Matthew Morin, is gay.

“One thing he said really stuck out to me,” she said. “He made that comment that, you know, he agreed with a lot of the sentiments that Albertans are feeling, but he didn't know if there was a place for him in [the vision of] Alberta that he was seeing from the leaders of the independence movement.”

“That was pretty eye-opening to me,” she said. “This movement will never be successful unless we can get the consensus from Albertans that we're all Albertans.”

“I hope people start being a little more gentle with each other … and now that this is over, that we can just start having more calmer conversations.”

Matthew Morin works in the social service sector and lives in Calgary. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

‘I think the world can become more volatile’

Morin, the author that Bayford mentioned, wrote a First Person column for CBC News about how the precarity of life today — and the feeling that those in charge don’t care — is fuelling his interest in independence.

He thought much of the support for separatism in Alberta should be seen as a protest vote. Reached after the referendum, he said that’s why he’s not surprised at the results.

“People are angry and that's why the nine questions got over 50 per cent or around 50 per cent. But they’re not angry enough to look to for separation.”

“So we'll see where it goes. 'Cause I think the world can become more volatile,” he said. “If the government doesn't actually enact any tangible change [to benefit people’s everyday lives], then people will just continue to get more frustrated and angry.”

Post-referendum, political analysts have been wondering how the referendum results will affect Premier Danielle Smith’s leadership, and if the committed separatists within her party will agitate to push her out.

Morin is not a committed separatist, but has been a Smith supporter. He door-knocked for her in the last election and joined the UCP so that he could vote for her leadership.

“I thought she was grassroots and would make a difference,” he said. “And she's made some differences. I mean, some differences were good and some were bad. That's with any politician.”

But at the moment, he doesn’t stand behind her the same way.

“In my ideal world, the government will use [this mandate] as a way to build policy that informs lower immigration, more control over crime, increasing affordable housing and building more housing, increasing funding for social programs and resources.

“And that they’d understand that people are just frustrated and instead of saying that everything's fine, maybe standing up on a podium and saying 'we hear you,' which is not really what I felt like I got from a lot of the politicians.”

Alex Krull in his garage in Fort McMurray. He says he hopes to stay involved with the independence movement and is proud of what it accomplished. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

‘We continue to be the rebel alliance’

Alex Krull came home after a 12-hour shift at an oilsands mine to catch the referendum results. He was disappointed votes in favour of having a binding referendum on separation didn’t hit 33 per cent, but still proud of everything the movement accomplished.

Earlier this fall, Prime Minister Mark Carney came to his workplace to announce the Pacific Link pipeline has been deemed to be in the national interest — and that’s due to the separatists’ agitation, he argues.

“It was very amusing as we're almost ground zero for separatism. A lot of us are high income, high tax paying, blue collar individuals. So we're definitely not your typical liberal supporters. But yeah, there he was.

“I've been following the mainstream media quite a bit since the referendum and they're completely dismissing the impact that our movement had on federal-provincial politics. They're saying things like the federal Liberals were already moving in this direction,” he said.

“I would strongly contend that. I think that our movement brought a lot of attention to the province, and we've seen a lot of capitulation from Ottawa on topics that I don't think we would have had, had we not had this form of rebellion.”

Krull volunteered with the independence campaign in Fort McMurray, collecting signatures to get the question on the ballot. The experience left him feeling that ordinary Albertans can make a difference, and he plans to stay involved, watching from the sidelines to see where he can help. That might be with a separatist party in the future, depending on how the political situation evolves, he said.

“Danielle Smith is in a dilly of a pickle ‘cause a big chunk of her support are separatist. So she's come out staunchly stating that the UCP going forward is a federalist party and that's how it is. So I think in 2027, Alberta, UCP has a big problem,” he said.

“But as far as the separatist movement, I think we continue to apply the pressure; we continue to be the rebel alliance against the Ottawa empire. Without that resistance, the status quo will overwhelm us, and I guess that's what democracy is.”

Brad Osadczuk ranches near Jenner, Alta. He says he supports provincial autonomy. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

‘If we’re not ready for change, we’re not ready for change’

Brad Osadczuk is a rancher near Jenner, Alta., about 200 kilometres east of Calgary. He was driving his empty cattle liner back from a feedlot, where he left a load of calves, when he took a phone call from CBC News.

Osadczuk is separatist curious. He says Monday’s results didn’t surprise him, but he was disappointed because he wanted to at least advance to the next step and have a serious look at what an independent Alberta could mean.

“I’m a businessman, so I like to see the details of a deal,” he said. “It may not ever work, [but] I would have loved to see what it would look like.”

Osadczuk spoke with CBC News during the campaign about his frustration with Ottawa — how much power is centralized in the east and how the bureaucracy is out of touch with the reality on the ground. He said he hopes this vote will help Alberta keep pushing for more authority.

“The feds see the results of this referendum, too,” he said. “I hope that maybe we can see some more goodwill and some work towards what Alberta would like out of this federation. I hope that there was a message sent.”

As for what happens next?

“We just keep living our lives. … If we’re not ready for change, we’re not ready for change.”

“I’m really sorry that people see this referendum as divisive. I see it as 100 per cent democracy. This was a government serving the people, not serving an agenda,” he said, adding that he hopes emotions will now settle down.

“I’m so tired of divisiveness.”

Daymond Khan, a member of the citizen action group at Southside Victory Church in Calgary, shared how his concerns over Canada's shifting identity have influenced his views on Alberta separatism. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

‘We can continue to stand for what's right’

During the campaign, Daymond Khan met with CBC News as part of a focus group at Southside Victory Church in Calgary, where he said the feeling that Canada was losing touch with its traditional Christian values pushed him to favour separatism.

But after the vote, he says he’s content with the outcome. He voted for Option 2, but never expected it to win and never wanted Alberta to actually leave.

“I'd like to see Alberta treated better within our federation, and I'd like to see the general direction of our nation and our federal government change,” he said.

And he’s already seeing positive signs.

“Economically, we see the federal support for the West Coast pipeline, which will hopefully help to turn the tide on seeing more major projects and investments in Canada,” he said. “Then on the moral side of things, we saw medical assistance in dying not get expanded to people who are just struggling with mental health challenges.

“I think that's a great decision by our leaders in Ottawa to not open that piece up.”

He believes the vote is giving Alberta more leverage. He says he takes to heart something Southside Victory’s Pastor Craig Buroker said recently in a sermon that the name Alberta is a variant of Albert, a name that means “noble and bright.”

“That was a good way to frame the calling of Alberta in our country and in general. So I'm confident that we can continue to stand for what's right and not necessarily be quiet about it.”

World.title: Canada needs concrete results from EU summit this week, former envoy says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ahead of this week's Canada-European Union summit in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney said both parties are hammering out a "new, ambitious alliance," after pledging deeper ties with Europe last month.

"An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves," Carney said in a written statement on Sunday. "An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices, and an alliance open enough that others can join.”

Former Liberal leader Stéphane Dion — who was special envoy to the EU from 2017 to 2025 — made clear that Canada needs to come out of this week's summit with nothing short of something tangible.

"What we need to see now is concrete results in all these files: trade, science, defence and security, artificial intelligence — concrete results of this partnership we have with the EU," Dion told CBC's David Common on Rosemary Barton Live Sunday morning.

"If it's, again, a kind of a communiqué at the end that would say 'we will continue to continue,' that would be very depressing."

Dion pointed to student and professional mobility between Canada and the EU as another area of improvement.

In his speech to the European Parliament last month, Carney showed clear interest in Erasmus+, a popular European exchange program that includes students and workers.

Stéphane Dion speaks to reporters at the Canadian Embassy in Paris on Feb. 10, 2025. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

Dion also said he wants to see action to put Canada's existing free trade deal with the EU — the Canada-European Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) — into full effect.

CETA was signed in 2016 and most of the agreement, aside from its investment chapter, took effect provisionally in 2017. All member states need to approve CETA for it to take full effect and, as of now, nine EU member states have not ratified the treaty in their respective legislatures : Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy and Poland.

Ahead of the summit, Canada and the EU are working on a digital trade agreement to ease business transactions across borders by smoothing frictions around e-signatures and e-contracts, paperless trade, secure cross-border data flows, duties on electronic transmissions and e-commerce.

A new kind of partnership

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the first "associate member" of the EU.

Carney welcomed the proposal's "ambition," but opted for the term "alliance of the future," when he spoke to the European Parliament a day later.

WATCH | Canadian ambassador after EU chief proposes 'associate' membership: Canadian ambassador focused on 'results' after EU chief opens door to associate membership | Duration closed caption 1:33 Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's incoming ambassador to the European Union, says 'we're not there' after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered to open the door to associate membership. 'What we're focused on is actually driving results,' he said, adding the government will 'eventually' turn to how to describe the relationship.

"I'm not sure that this expression of an associate membership will fly," Dion said, noting that the term is up against resistance both in Canada and Europe.

"It sounds like if Canada was sending part of its sovereignty to Brussels, and there is no appetite for that in Canada," Dion continued. "In Europe, it's like if Canada would have the advantages of the union without the obligations that come with it regarding financing, regarding regulation alignment."

Dion instead suggested Canada could become an "official observer," offering reciprocity to the bloc while protecting Canadian interests. Observers have a limited membership where they can't vote or fill an elected position within the European Parliament's organization.

He also said an improvement to the Canada-EU partnership would be full membership in the European Political Community, a forum where European countries beyond the member states meet twice a year.

Dion said the European Political Community "would welcome Prime Minister Carney as the most European of non-European countries," and Canada could take part without commitments like financing or regulatory alignment.

World.title: Venezuela's opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela on Sunday for the first time since December, returning from exile at a time when doubts about the country's democratic future — and the role of the U.S. — are growing.

It was her first appearance since the U.S. military deposed the country's then-president Nicolás Maduro in January, replacing him with an interim president who has exceeded the time she was authorized to serve, with no election scheduled.

Machado announced her arrival on social media, writing: "I am here. With you."

Another leading figure in the Venezuelan opposition, Edmundo Gonzalez, wrote on X confirming that Machado had arrived and that he would be next to her "very soon."

"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" he wrote. "You know it, this is until the end."

Supporters greet Machado

On Sunday afternoon, Machado strode into a church in the state of Lara, west of Caracas, to the applause of dozens gathered there as they shook her hand and hugged her, with cellphones aloft to record her return.

"María! María!" someone cried out, as another shouted, "Welcome to Venezuela!"

"Long live freedom, damn it!" a man yelled.

One woman wiped away tears and called it "a miracle," while another woman's hands flew to her face as she saw Machado enter the church.

Asked by reporters Sunday about Machado's return to Venezuela, U.S. President Donald Trump said: "I don't know anything about it, but I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe. She's a very nice woman. But we're doing really well in Venezuela."

No election scheduled

Since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela has been run by interim President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally who received the Trump administration's blessing to succeed him.

Rodríguez was initially supposed to serve only 90 days as acting president, but has remained in office and has made no move to call an election.

Machado went into hiding in Venezuela for 11 months after being briefly detained following a protest in January 2025.

WATCH | Machado was awarded the Nobel peace prize last year: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader | Duration 1:51 The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Maria Corina Machado. Machado won 'for her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and for her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy,' the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in its citation.

After leaving the country in a clandestine escape, she reappeared that December in Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her peaceful challenge to Maduro's authoritarian government.

Machado and her allies have been demanding a date for a presidential election in Venezuela, but U.S. officials have emphasized economic stabilization first.

Election integrity questioned

In October 2023, Machado won an opposition primary and intended to challenge Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but the government barred her from running for office.

González took her place on the ballot, and ample credible evidence showed that he defeated Maduro by more than a 2 to 1 margin. But the National Electoral Council, which is stacked with ruling-party loyalists, declared Maduro the winner.

The lead-up and aftermath of the election were marked by widespread government repression, including forced disappearances, torture and other human rights violations. More than 2,000 people, including poll workers, were detained in the days after the vote.

WATCH | Detractors decry Maduro's 2024 election win: Upset Venezuelans react as Maduro claims presidency | Duration 1:04 Winning a third term with 51 per cent of the vote, incumbent Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro stated he would defend the democracy and people of Venezuela, while detractors voiced their unhappiness with the election results after multiple exit polls suggested the opposition would win.

In January, the U.S. military captured Maduro in Caracas and whisked him to New York to face drug-related charges, which he has denied. Many Venezuelans were stunned by the Trump administration's decision to work with Rodríguez, instead of Machado, to try to revitalize the crisis-racked country.

Machado had repeatedly vowed to return to Venezuela, and, according to her party, she made seven unsuccessful attempts.

One of the efforts would have seen her take a charter boat, but the operator cancelled the trip, alleging the vessel was unfit for navigation. In another attempt, her team said, Machado tried to fly to the Caribbean island of Curacao, from where she could take a speedboat to Venezuela, but her plane was denied landing permits.

Opposition activists have accused Venezuela's government of blocking Machado's return, a claim denied by Venezuelan authorities. Others have also questioned whether the Trump administration has also been involved in the efforts to stop her from returning.

Trump administration officials deny they are holding Machado back but have said that, on some occasions, they have advised her against returning due to safety concerns.

After Maduro was deposed, Venezuela's highest court said Rodríguez could serve as acting president for up to 90 days — an interim appointment that could be extended by the National Assembly for an additional 90 days. But the ruling party-controlled assembly never voted to extend her term.

WATCH | Who is interim President Delcy Rodríguez?: Who is Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodriguez? | Duration closed caption 4:00 With Nicolás Maduro removed from office, Delcy Rodriguez has become Venezuela’s interim president. CBC’s Lyndsay Duncombe breaks down Rodriguez’s rise and the complicated relationship she’s entered with the U.S. government.

Machado and her allies have demanded that the Rodríguez government set a date for a presidential election. Rodríguez told the UN General Assembly in September that Venezuelans will determine the "right moment" for the next election.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has argued that before holding new elections, Venezuela must stabilize its economy and rebuild its institutions, including its courts and electoral council. But he said in a news conference earlier this month that Machado has "every right to enter her country whenever she wants to return."

Supporters of Machado have held demonstrations in Caracas demanding her return.
