World.title: From the Ganges to the Danube: Why Mukesh Srivastava fell in love with Hungary – Exclusive interview
World.content:
From the Ganges to the Danube, Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s journey in Hungary became far more than a diplomatic posting. Having completed her tenure as director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest, he returned to India from Hungary – the country where his child was born – with unforgettable memories, lasting friendships and a deep personal connection. In an exclusive interview with Daily News Hungary, Dr Srivastava reflects on his love for Hungary, his experiences learning the Hungarian language, the growing cultural ties between India and Hungary, and why Budapest will always feel like a second home.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): As you have concluded your tenure as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest and returned to India, how do you look back on your time in Hungary?

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava: I look back on my time in Hungary with immense gratitude, a deep sense of fulfilment and countless cherished memories. Serving as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre was both an honour and a privilege. For me, it was much more than a professional assignment; it was a beautiful journey of cultural exchange, lasting friendships, learning and personal growth.

What I will treasure most are the people I have met along the way. I have had the privilege of interacting with remarkable Hungarian artists, scholars, Indologists, students, cultural practitioners, Yoga enthusiasts, Ayurveda experts, journalists, and other countless friends of India, as well as the vibrant Indian community in Hungary. Their warmth, enthusiasm and genuine affection made my journey truly special. Through these interactions, I witnessed how culture has the extraordinary power to bring people together, transcending differences of language, geography and traditions.

Hungary also holds a deeply personal place in my heart, as my child was born in Budapest. The city will therefore always be part of our family’s story and most precious memories.

Now that I have returned to India, I look back with a sense of professional satisfaction, but also with the emotions that come from leaving behind a place that became so close to my heart. I have brought home enduring friendships, wonderful memories and a firm belief that the cultural relations between India and Hungary will continue to grow stronger in the years ahead.

DNH: What were your first impressions of Budapest, Hungary when you arrived?

Srivastava: My first impression of Budapest was of a remarkably beautiful and historic city. The majestic Danube, magnificent architecture, iconic Parliament Building, elegant bridges and rich cultural heritage captivated me from the very beginning.

What particularly struck me was the wonderful balance between old-world charm and modernity. Budapest is a cosmopolitan city with a vibrant cultural and social life, yet it retains a very strong sense of its history and traditions. I admired the respect Hungarians have for their heritage, culture and language, as well as their deep appreciation for arts.

Over time, however, Budapest became much more than a beautiful city. I began to discover its people, artistic traditions, intellectual life and sense of history. I also came to appreciate the warmth, resilience and creativity of Hungarians. Initially, I saw Hungary largely through the eyes of a visitor; gradually, I began to experience it as a home.

DNH: What was the first year like for you, both professionally and personally?

Srivastava: The first year was a period of adjustment, discovery, and learning, both professionally and personally.

Professionally, there was much to explore and understand—the Hungarian cultural landscape, the interests and perspectives of the local community, the institutional environment, and how best to present Indian culture in ways that would resonate with the Hungarian people.

Personally, adapting to a new country and a different rhythm of life brought learning experiences and rewarding discoveries. The warmth and hospitality of the Hungarian people made the transition much easier.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Looking back at your time in Hungary, how have you seen the cultural relationship between India and Hungary evolve?

Srivastava: During my tenure, I have witnessed a meaningful and encouraging evolution in the cultural relationship between India and Hungary. What has impressed me most is the growing sense of mutual understanding, appreciation and curiosity among people from both nations.

There has been increasing interest in Indian art, literature, classical music, dance and cinema. However, what stands out most is the remarkable popularity of Yoga and Ayurveda, particularly for their holistic health and well-being benefits. This growing interest is also reflected in the increasing presence of Yoga and Ayurveda institutions across Hungary.

I have also observed that cultural exchange is becoming more reciprocal and collaborative. Beyond showcasing Indian culture and traditions in Hungary, artists, institutions and communities from both countries are increasingly coming together to share ideas, celebrate their heritage and build lasting connections.

The cultural and community activities during my time in Hungary have reinforced that the strongest bonds between nations are often built through people-to-people connections; it is also about the friendships, shared experiences and mutual understanding that remain long after an event has concluded.

Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest and the Liszt Cultural Institute in New Delhi have played significant roles in strengthening cultural relations between the two countries, providing continuity to cultural engagement and transforming programmes into enduring relationships.

DNH: Which event, programme or initiative organised during your tenure are you most proud of, and why?

Srivastava: It is difficult to single out just one programme, as every successful initiative was the result of collective effort, dedication and teamwork. What made these experiences truly special was the opportunity to bring people together, encourage cultural dialogue and strengthen the bonds of friendship between India and Hungary.

Several initiatives remain particularly close to my heart: India Knowledge Series, which introduced Hungarian audiences to India’s rich cultural heritage, philosophy and traditions through lectures and discussions in the Hungarian language; Yoga at Liberty bridge, unique experience of Yoga on a moving cruise along the Danube, Indian Film Festival at Budapest’s historic Puskin Cinema, 100+ Yoga events organised across Hungary as part of the International Day of Yoga (IDY) 2026; and the School and college Connect Programme, which brought Indian culture closer to young Hungarian students.

However, one initiative of which I am particularly proud is the proposed establishment of a statue of Swami Vivekananda at Széchenyi István University in Győr. I am deeply grateful that the University leadership graciously accepted the proposal of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre, Embassy of India and extended its support for installing the statue at a prominent location on the University campus, continuing its longstanding support for our cultural initiatives.

I sincerely believe that, once realised, this initiative will not only honour the legacy of Swami Vivekananda but also serve as an enduring symbol of India–Hungary friendship, inspiring future generations and further strengthening the cultural and intellectual ties between our two nations.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Were there any moments when you felt that Hungarian audiences connected with Indian culture in a particularly meaningful way?

Srivastava: Absolutely. There were many unforgettable moments when I witnessed the genuine warmth and appreciation of Hungarian audiences for Indian culture.

One particularly touching experience was this year’s Indian Film Festival at Puskin Cinema in Budapest. After the final screening, the audience responded with such tremendous enthusiasm that the applause seemed endless. What moved me even more was that several people personally approached me to thank for the festival and share how much they had enjoyed the films. At that moment, I felt how beautifully Indian cinema could touch hearts and bring people together beyond language and borders.

Another memorable moment was the Yoga event at Budapest’s Liberty Bridge in 2024. Seeing the bridge filled with people practising Yoga together was extraordinary. I felt the same spirit during the IDY celebrations at Dr. Koltai Jenő Sportközpont at the Hungarian University of Sports Science, where people of different ages and backgrounds came together in a shared spirit of harmony and well-being. It was a powerful reminder of how an ancient Indian tradition has become an integral part of everyday life in Hungary.

What was most striking is the genuine love and respect that so many Hungarians have for Indian culture, Hindu philosophy and spiritual traditions. Their enthusiasm for Yoga, Ayurveda, Indian festivals, ancient wisdom and spiritual heritage is truly remarkable. Krishna Valley in Somogyvámos is a wonderful example of how Indian spiritual traditions and philosophy have taken deep root in Hungary, reflecting this profound cultural connection.

During my tenure, I met many Hungarians whose knowledge and understanding of Indian philosophy and traditions are extraordinary. One of my most meaningful experiences was the personal conversations after cultural events, when Hungarian audience shared their appreciation for Indian culture and often discovered similarities with their own values and culture.

DNH: How could cultural, educational and people-to-people ties between Hungary and India be strengthened further?

Srivastava: We should invest even more in sustained exchanges rather than one-time events. Artist residencies, University partnerships, student exchanges, joint research, translation projects, collaborations between museums and cultural institutions, and opportunities for young artists would all be valuable.

Hungarian Indologists, artists, and practitioners who have dedicated themselves to the study, preservation, and promotion of Indian culture, traditions, and heritage should also receive greater encouragement and support. Their invaluable contributions reflect the depth and vitality of the people-to-people ties that have long enriched relations between India and Hungary.

There is also considerable scope for greater engagement beyond Budapest and beyond the major institutions. Digital platforms can help connect audiences, but physical interaction remains extremely important. When students, artists, academics and people from all walks of life spend time in each other’s countries, they develop a deeper mutual understanding that cannot be achieved through formal diplomacy alone.

DNH: What was everyday life like in Budapest for you and your family?

Srivastava: Everyday life gradually developed its own rhythm. Budapest is a city where history and modern life coexist beautifully. We enjoyed walking along the Danube, discovering different parts of the city, visiting cultural institutions and simply observing everyday Hungarian life.

One of the things I particularly enjoyed was the Danube. Coming from Varanasi, where the Ganges River is such an important part of life and identity, looking at the Danube often reminded me of the Ganges in Varanasi. Of course, the two rivers are very different in their character and history, but both have a powerful presence in the life and imagination of the people living along their banks. That created a very personal connection for me.

Living abroad also teaches you to appreciate small things—local neighbourhoods, familiar cafés like Vaj at Hello Buda and Mandragora near Batthyány tér, public transport, seasonal changes, food and conversations with friends you meet regularly. Over time, these experiences become some of your strongest memories of a place.

During my tenure, I was fortunate to make wonderful friends who stood behind me like pillars of support. Their friendship and kindness made my life easier, happier and much more enjoyable.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: During your time in Hungary, you often expressed your deep affection and respect for the Hungarian people and their culture, frequently greeting audiences in Hungarian during your speeches and even delivering messages in the language at national celebrations, International Day of Yoga events and other cultural occasions. Given that Hungarian is widely regarded as a particularly challenging language for foreigners, how did you approach learning it, and what did the experience mean to you personally?

Srivastava: Learning Hungarian was certainly challenging, but equally rewarding. I have always believed that making an effort to speak the language of a country is not only a gesture of respect but also a genuine way to connect with people and understand their culture.

I approached it with patience, curiosity and determination, beginning with simple phrases and gradually gaining confidence. Over time, I realised that even a few words spoken sincerely in someone’s native language could create a special connection.

Speaking Hungarian on occasions such as Hungary’s State Foundation Day, International Day of Yoga celebrations, the Indian Film Festival and, finally, in my farewell video was my way of expressing my affection and respect for the Hungarian people and their language.

Although I am far from fluent, the response I received was overwhelmingly encouraging. For me, the Hungarian language became another beautiful bridge connecting me with the people and culture I deeply admire.

Simply put, I love Hungary and its language.

If you missed it: Youngest Indian diplomat Dr. Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s Hungarian farewell message draws widespread public appreciation

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Apart from your cherished memories and friendships, what is one thing you have brought back with you from Hungary to India?

Srivastava: Beyond the wonderful memories and enduring friendships, one of the most valuable things I have brought back from Hungary is a deep appreciation for the way Hungarians cherish their cultural heritage and the dedication with which they preserve and pass it on to future generations.

I have also been deeply inspired by the spirit of collaboration among Hungarian artists, scholars and cultural practitioners. My experiences in Hungary reinforced my belief that tradition and innovation are not opposing forces; rather, they can complement and enrich each other, keeping cultural heritage alive while embracing new ideas and perspectives.

DNH: How would you describe the Indian community in Hungary today and its role in preserving and promoting India’s rich cultural heritage?

Srivastava: The Indian community in Hungary is vibrant, diverse and deeply connected to its cultural roots. During my tenure, I witnessed a strong sense of preservation of Indian traditions while embracing Hungarian society and culture.

Festivals such as Holi, Diwali, Navratri and various regional celebrations bring families and younger generations together, keeping our rich cultural heritage alive. The community also enthusiastically shares these traditions with Hungarian friends.

Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre provided an important platform for such cultural exchanges, while community-led initiatives further strengthened the cultural bonds between India and Hungary.

DNH: Now that you have concluded your tenure in Budapest and returned to India, what message would you like to share with the people of Hungary?

Srivastava: My message is simple, but it comes from the bottom of my heart: Thank you for everything.

I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the Government and people of Hungary, my Hungarian friends and everyone who contributed to strengthening the cultural bonds between India and Hungary. Your warmth, generosity, support and friendship made my journey truly unforgettable.

Hungary was my first overseas posting, and it will always hold a special place in my heart. I arrived to share India’s rich cultural heritage and returned with something precious: lasting friendships, beautiful memories and a deep affection for Hungary and its people.

Although I have returned to India, the friendships and connections I built remain as meaningful as ever. I sincerely hope to return one day, not merely as a former Director, but as a friend.

I firmly believe that the cultural bonds between India and Hungary will continue to flourish, bringing our people even closer together.

In hindsight, my tenure in Hungary may have come to an end, but the bond I have built with this country and its people will last a lifetime.

Until we meet again – Viszontlátásra !!

World.title: Op-ed – The invisible transition: Hungary’s new government and Europe’s old rules
World.content:
Péter Magyar has inherited a luxury most European leaders can only dream of: a kétharmad, Hungary’s politically formidable two-thirds parliamentary majority. After sixteen years, Viktor Orbán is out of power, and Hungary’s new prime minister has the votes to rewrite much of the country’s political rulebook. Unfortunately for him, Brussels plays by another set of rules. Winning an election does not automatically come with the keys to the European treasury.

Guest post by Costantino Pistilli

On 23 September, the European Commission proposed lifting financial measures imposed on Hungary in 2022, potentially releasing €4.2 billion in cohesion funding and restoring access to Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe for affected institutions. Brussels acknowledged progress on public procurement, anti-corruption safeguards and conflicts of interest. On 13 October, the Council approved the lifting of those measures. After years of disputes, Budapest finally had more than a promise: the restrictions were removed, although other financial conditions remain.

The European machinery has hardly slowed down. At the General Affairs Council in Luxembourg that same day, EU ministers examined Hungary’s position under Article 7 of the EU Treaty, the procedure launched in 2018 over rule-of-law concerns. Budapest outlined reforms already undertaken and further measures planned, while ministers also discussed the EU’s 2028–2034 budget. The meeting offered Magyar an early institutional test before his European partners. The financial breakthrough did not close the separate Article 7 procedure. Governments change. Brussels keeps its files.

For Magyar, the challenge is unusual. He has the parliamentary strength to dismantle much of Orbán’s institutional legacy, but must prove that the replacements will be independent of his own government. Replacing those in charge is relatively easy. Persuading them to respect limits on their power is another matter.

Some changes are already under way. In June, Parliament amended the Constitution to introduce an eight-year limit on the premiership. A broader constitutional amendment followed in July, addressing senior state institutions, the judiciary and the rules governing key legislation. These measures demonstrate Magyar’s willingness to use his supermajority. Whether they produce institutions less dependent on political power is a more demanding question.

If you missed it – Reuters: Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project

Consider the public-interest foundations established under Orbán, whose governance became a central issue in the dispute over European funding. Transparent appointments, independent audits and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules could help protect them from political interference. The same applies to public procurement: open competition and effective oversight would give Hungarian businesses a better chance of winning contracts without the right political connections. A two-thirds majority makes passing legislation easier. Earning public trust takes rather more than a parliamentary vote.

Poland offers a useful warning. Donald Tusk returned to government in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence, only to discover how controversial the methods of institutional repair could become. Magyar faces a similar dilemma: how to dismantle a system of political control without building another one, merely changing who gives the orders.

For ordinary Hungarians, the consequences extend well beyond constitutional arguments. The Council’s decision has made €4.2 billion in cohesion funding available again, potentially supporting regional infrastructure and development. It has also reopened Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe opportunities for students and researchers at affected institutions. Yet other restrictions remain: approximately €3.5 billion in cohesion funding is subject to separate EU conditions. Unlocking one part of the money does not mean collecting the entire amount.

The next EU budget adds another complication. On 10 October, Ireland’s presidency of the Council presented a revised negotiating proposal for the 2028–2034 financial framework. Agriculture, regional development, competitiveness and security are competing for resources. Hungary will need practical allies, including countries such as Italy, which also have substantial interests in agricultural and cohesion funding. Political friendships help, but when billions are being divided, every capital reaches for its calculator.

Brussels, meanwhile, has its own credibility to defend. If Hungary meets the agreed conditions, its progress must be recognised regardless of who governs in Budapest. Otherwise, the suspicion that European funding depends partly on political sympathies will only grow. The standards applied to Orbán must also apply to Magyar. Equally, an electoral victory cannot erase unresolved legal concerns.

Hungary’s transition is therefore a test for both sides. Magyar can change institutions, while Brussels retains the authority to assess reforms and enforce financial conditions. The new prime minister must resist the temptation to inherit Orbán’s powers along with his office. The European Union must demonstrate that its rules remain consistent when the political landscape changes.

Magyar has achieved what once seemed improbable: replacing Orbán after sixteen years. His supermajority gives him the means to reshape Hungary, but also deprives him of a convenient excuse if reforms fail. The real achievement would be institutions capable of functioning independently when that majority is gone. Brussels, having demanded such independence for years, will have to demonstrate that it knows how to recognise it.



*Costantino Pistilli is an Italian geopolitical analyst and author. His work has appeared in the Daily Express, Comment Central and Defensa.com. He has also contributed research and analysis to New Direction.

World.title: More Chinese flights from Budapest cancelled as airlines suspend routes – what could be behind the cuts?
World.content:
More Chinese flights from Budapest are facing cancellations and temporary suspensions, raising questions about the profitability of long-haul connections between Hungary and China. Following changes to Hainan Airlines’ Shenzhen service, China Eastern Airlines and Shanghai Airlines are reportedly cutting flights to Ningbo and suspending their Xi’an route for several months.

Chinese flights from Budapest face further cancellations

According to information published by Hungarian aviation news outlet Budflyer and subsequently reported by Világgazdaság, several previously scheduled flights between Ningbo, a major commercial and industrial city in eastern China, and Budapest will not operate in November and December 2026.

The affected dates are:

November 2026: 5, 9, 12 and 16

December 2026: 3 and 14

The route is operated by Shanghai Airlines, part of the China Eastern Airlines group.

However, some third-party flight databases continue to display departures on certain affected dates. The cancellations should therefore be treated as reported schedule changes rather than independently confirmed cancellations of every listed service.

Xi’an–Budapest route reportedly suspended until February 2027

A more substantial interruption is expected on the Xi’an–Budapest route.

According to the same reports, the once-weekly direct service will be suspended from 7 November 2026 until 26 February 2027, leaving the two cities without their regular nonstop passenger connection for several months.

Xi’an, the capital of Shaanxi province and the historical starting point of the Silk Road, is an important cultural, educational and economic centre in north-western China.

The reported suspension could affect tourists, business travellers and passengers visiting friends and relatives. However, the precise duration of the interruption has not yet been independently confirmed through an official airline statement.

Hainan Airlines also reduces its Budapest operations

The latest developments follow significant adjustments by Hainan Airlines.

As AIRportal.hu reported on 16 October, Hainan’s Shenzhen–Budapest flights have been removed from booking systems between 16 and 30 November.

Services could resume on 4 December, although the airline’s schedules for the remaining winter months remain uncertain.

Hainan Airlines is also reducing or suspending services on several other European routes, including connections to Vienna, Brussels and Madrid.

These changes indicate that the adjustments extend beyond Budapest and form part of a broader revision of the carrier’s international operations.

If you missed it: Exclusive interview – Chinese Ambassador: Hungary-China ties on a ‘steady track’ as Budapest emerges as a potential robotics hub

Why are Chinese flights from Budapest being reduced?

Neither China Eastern Airlines nor Shanghai Airlines has publicly provided a detailed explanation for the reported cancellations. Hainan Airlines has also not officially confirmed the specific commercial reasons behind its latest schedule changes.

Nevertheless, several economic and operational factors could explain why airlines might reduce their long-haul capacity.

– High aviation fuel costs: Long-haul flights consume substantial quantities of fuel, making their profitability particularly sensitive to changes in global energy prices. Higher operating costs can make routes with limited margins less attractive.

– Insufficient passenger demand: If flights fail to attract enough paying passengers, or if average ticket revenues are too low, operating the service may become financially unsustainable. However, there is currently no publicly verified evidence that low booking numbers are responsible for these particular cancellations.

– Withdrawal of financial or marketing support: Some international air routes benefit from promotional agreements or financial incentives during their development. According to AIRportal.hu, earlier Chinese media reports linked previous Hainan Airlines route reductions to the withdrawal of support. Whether this directly contributed to the latest Budapest changes remains unconfirmed.

– Seasonal fluctuations in travel demand: Airlines frequently adjust capacity during the winter season, particularly on routes where leisure travel represents a significant share of passengers.

– Aircraft and network optimisation: Carriers may redeploy aircraft to routes offering stronger demand, higher yields or better connections through their main hubs.

Importantly, these are possible commercial explanations, not confirmed reasons for the individual route suspensions. No verified passenger load figures or route-level financial results have been published to establish whether the Budapest services were operating at a loss.

What does this mean for Budapest Airport and passengers?

Hungary has developed extensive direct air connections with China in recent years, supported by growing economic cooperation, Chinese investment and tourism.

Direct flights are particularly valuable for business travellers because they eliminate the need to transfer through other European, Middle Eastern or Asian hubs.

The reported reductions do not mean that direct air travel between Hungary and China is coming to an end. Nevertheless, they highlight how individual routes remain exposed to changing market conditions and airline commercial decisions.

Passengers booked on affected Chinese flights from Budapest should check their reservation status directly with the operating airline or travel agency. Where a flight has been cancelled, travellers should request information about alternative connections, refunds and any applicable passenger rights.

For now, the key question is whether the changes represent a temporary winter adjustment or the beginning of a longer-term reduction in capacity. The airlines’ subsequent schedule updates will provide a clearer picture.

World.title: Court remands former central bank gov Matolcsy into custody
World.content:
The Budapest Central District Court on Friday remanded Gyorgy Matolcsy, the former governor of the National Bank of Hungary (NBH), into custody for one month.

The court ordered the detention on suspicion of graft and use of forged documents, Anna Madarasi, a spokesperson for the court, said.

Madarasi said the court also ordered the 30-day detention of the representative who acted during the conclusion of the loan agreement – which forms the basis of the suspicion – as well as a lawyer involved in the securities transaction, Mihaly Valko and Tamas Sandor. She noted that György Matolcsy did not provide a statement, nor did the other two suspects.

The court found that there were well-founded concerns regarding the suspects — specifically the risk of them absconding, going into hiding, interfering with the proceedings, or reoffending — and concluded that no less restrictive coercive measure would be appropriate. The court also entertained no doubts regarding the well-founded suspicion that a crime had been committed or the financial loss that had been incurred, the spokesperson stated.

If you missed it – Prosecutors seek to arrest former Hungarian central bank chief Matolcsy – UPDATE: video of arrival at prison

She also said that the prosecutor’s office has requested the issuance of European and international arrest warrants for Adam Matolcsy, as well as for Gyorgy Stofa, the head of the companies managing the assets of the NBH foundations.

Following appeals filed by the suspects and their defence counsel, the court order for their arrest is not yet final, the spokesperson said.

Matolcsy was detained for questioning on Wednesday by the Central Chief Prosecution Office of Investigation (KNYF) on suspicion of financial fraud and the use of forged documents.

The KNYF said it had taken action regarding the attempted transfer of control, under a sham securities lending agreement, of assets in the central bank’s PADME Foundation to a group of people over whom Matolcsy would have influence after his mandate as central bank governor ended. The aim of the agreement, signed a day before the governor’s term ended, was to enable Matolcsy and his son to use the assets for investments for their own gain, it added.

The resulting financial loss cannot be precisely calculated at present, but is “well over” the HUF 500m threshold for a “particularly significant financial loss”, the KNYF said.

World.title: ‘Collective Fear’: Pressure on Serbians with Disabilities to Vote for Ruling Party
World.content:
According to Serbia’s 2022 census, more than 356,000 people with disabilities in Serbia, or roughly 5.5 per cent of the population over the age of two.

For years, Serbian election authorities have been criticised for failing to ensure voting privacy for people with disabilities, such as those living with blindness or vision impairment who are not provided with braille ballot papers; international election observers have previously cited the inaccessibility of polling stations for people with disabilities.

Political pressure on socially vulnerable voters in Serbia has been documented before.

In a 2023 report, election watchdog CRTA identified networks of political influence within social welfare centres and collected accounts from employees describing the use of social assistance to secure political support, including votes and participation in party activities.

CRTA’s monitoring of the 2023 elections also documented a case in which beneficiaries of social welfare support were denied that support for supporting an opposition party.

According to 2021 data from the association Creative-educational centre, people with disabilities and their families are among those at highest risk of poverty, with over 70 per cent of families living below the poverty line and only 13 per cent of people with disabilities in work.

Many people with disabilities are dependent on state welfare support – financial as well as in healthcare support and services – and on associations that usually provide help with access to assistive devices, education, training and employment.

Out of a dozen people interviewed by BIRN for this story, five reported witnessing statements from representatives of these associations that could be interpreted as pressure to vote for the SNS.

A person from a disability organisation in southern Serbia said the recently appointed head of the organisation had asked others within the organisation to pledge their vote for the ruling party and its candidate for prime minister, ex-President Aleksandar Vucic.

“I was present at the assembly when she was elected president,” the person said. “Afterwards, she told several people to stay because she wanted to ask them something. She then took each of them outside individually, including my neighbour. When my neighbour returned, I asked her what she had been asked. She told me she had immediately realised what it was about – whether she was willing to pledge her support to Vucic and the SNS as a secure vote.”

Many of these organisations are dependent on funding from public coffers.

Another person from a Belgrade-based organisation said such pressure is commonplace.

“We receive threats that our funding will be cut,” the person said.

World.title: Proposed Law to Curb Powers of Hague-Based Court Returned to Kosovo Assembly
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Supporters of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leader and former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci take part in a march in support of him in Pristina, Kosovo, prior to the verdict, September 12, 2026. EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula sent the amended Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) bill back to parliament on Thursday for review on the request of the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) which had proposed the bill, less than three weeks after its controversial approval.

The law, which aims to curtail the jurisdiction of the Hague-based court, came after weeks of street protests led by Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) veterans, who rallied under the slogan “Not in my name” – a reference to the KSC judge’s choice of words, “In the name of the people of Kosovo”, when he read the verdict.

“The president received a formal proposal from the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo – the sponsor of the legislation – to allow the assembly to reconsider the law, specifically the provisions concerning the jurisdiction and mandate of the Specialist Chambers,” read a statement from the president’s office on Thursday.

“The president has reiterated her opposition to any attempt to distort the historical truth of Kosovo, to cast doubt on the liberationist nature of the war, or to equate the people who fought for freedom and survival with the regime that oppressed them,” the statement read.

The initial bill was passed after four former KLA leaders were convicted by the KSC for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed between April 1998 and June 1999.

Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years, respectively, with credit for time served in detention from November 2020. The verdict can be appealed and their lawyers are working to challenge the conviction.

Given the uncertainty over whether the KSC will indict anyone else, the effect of the bill is uncertain, but the message it sent was clear, and the European Union was unhappy.

“The Law […] goes against Kosovo’s international obligations towards the EU,” read a statement from the EU after the law was initially approved. The EU finances most of the court’s operations.

In a speech at the Berlin Process Summit in Montenegro on Thursday, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that “weeks and months of defining moments” lie ahead for the Western Balkans and reminded Kosovo of its obligations under international law.

On Thursday, Perparim Gruda, a MP from PDK who was involved in drafting the recent KSC bill wrote on Facebook that “there is no error in the law amending the Law on the Specialist Chambers.”

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court, part of Kosovo’s judiciary but located in The Hague and staffed by internationals. The court was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. Hashim Thaci was one of the main Kosovar supporters of the establishment of the court.

Since the conviction of the former KLA leaders over a month ago, criticism of the KSC has continued unabated in Kosovo. On October 14, Kosovo’s Ombudsperson, Naim Qelaj, held an event in Pristina to demand external oversight of the KSC.

Qelaj claimed that the court “has not been subject to democratic monitoring and control by the institutions of the Republic of Kosovo, creating a lack of transparency and accountability towards the citizens and institutions of Kosovo”.

He said it should report to the Kosovo authorities and that the Ombudsperson institution should be able to have access to its work.

KSC spokesperson Angela Griep told BIRN that “according to the legal framework of the Specialist Chambers, the Kosovo Ombudsperson does not have any responsibility with respect to the Specialist Chambers. This responsibility falls exclusively with the Ombudsperson of the Specialist Chambers in accordance with the Kosovo Constitution”.

World.title: One Dead, Crew Members Missing After Ship Sinks off Romania
World.content:
A Romanian navy squad during NATO naval drill ‘Sea Shield 24’ on the Black Sea, off the coast of Constanta, Romania, 16 April 2024. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT

Romanian maritime authorities launched a rescue operation on Friday morning about 24 kilometres off the coast after a vessel was reportedly struck by a drone.

Rescuers are continuing to search for three missing crew members, according to preliminary reports.

The circumstances of the incident remain unclear, including the origin of the drone and whether the vessel was deliberately targeted.

President Nicusor Dan reacted swiftly to the incident, saying that it “is another event in the process of escalation that Russia is pursuing in the Black Sea region.”

The sinking follows an incident on October 15 when two other commercial ships were hit overnight while anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube-Black Sea Canal, a major shipping route used to transport Ukrainian goods. Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have been a frequent target of Russian attacks.

Similar incidents have also occurred in Bulgarian territorial waters, where drone strikes have reportedly left at least 23 sailors dead or missing.

The escalating tensions in the Black Sea have prompted NATO to announce increased surveillance in the region following recent attacks on commercial vessels.

Meanwhile, Romania has proposed that it join Bulgaria and Turkey, the other two NATO member states bordering the Black Sea, in establishing a joint military command to be led by the three countries on a rotational basis.

World.title: Alleged Police Violence Against Minors Alarms Albania
World.content:
In a video shared on Monday evening, a group of police officers can be seen rushing towards several young people and beating them with batons. Amid the blows, one of them can be heard shouting that he is only 13 years old.

BIRN was unable to independently verify the ages of the young people in the video, but similar footage showing police in Tirana using violence against protesters, including minors, has circulated widely in the media and on social media over the past week.

The footage has raised concerns about how the State Police is treating children and teenagers involved in the wave of protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government.

World.title: Serbia Braces for Most Uncertain Elections in 14 Years
World.content:
On Sunday, Serbia is bracing for what could be its most uncertain and high-stakes elections in 14 years, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, facing a challenge that has emerged out of a two-year student-led protest movement.

Since 2012, Aleksandar Vucic and his party SNS have largely dominated the political and electoral landscape. This time, however, the election outcome is far less predictable, political analysts say, as the student movement has reshaped the opposition landscape and mobilised supporters well beyond the established parties.

“These are the first elections in a long time whose outcome is entirely uncertain,” Nebojsa Vladisavljevic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade, told BIRN.

World.title: He Survived a Shipwreck and Built a Church – 900 Years Later, Croatia Officially Protected it
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – A merchant surviving a shipwreck and then building a church in gratitude that Croatia officially chose to protect almost 1,000 years later is the story behind a construction on an island few know about.

It’s believed that the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian (Crvka sv. Kuzme i Damjana) on the island of Ugljan dates from the 11th or 12th century. It is located in a peaceful cove, right by the sea, not far from the hamlet of Guduće. Olive groves, dense pine forests, beautiful coves, old fishing villages, crystal-clear sea and views of the Zadar archipelago are what await visitors to Ugljan.

As Ivana Vasarevic writes for Putni Kofer, it’s widely known as one of Croatia’s greenest islands, which also carries the flattering nickname “the garden of Zadar.” It’s just 22 kilometres long, has a little over 5,600 inhabitants, is separated from the mainland by the Zadar Channel, and is connected to the neighbouring island of Pašman by a bridge across the Ždrelac passage. Among Ugljan’s main attractions is the fortress of St. Michael above Preko; nearby is also the islet of Galevac, known for its Franciscan monastery, while in Muline you can visit the remains of an ancient oil mill where the Liburnian olive oil was once produced.

TODAY IT IS CONSIDERED THE OLDEST PRESERVED CHURCH IN THE SETTLEMENT OF UGLJAN

The island’s special charm comes from its small stone churches. One of them was recently declared a cultural asset by the Ministry of Culture and Media of the Republic of Croatia. It is the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, located in Ljokine Cove, not far from the hamlet of Guduće, on the southwestern side of the island. This modest stone building stands right on the shore and is the oldest preserved church in the settlement of Ugljan: it is believed to date from the 11th or 12th century.

Besides its exceptional historical value, the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian is also interesting because of the unusual legend that has accompanied it for centuries. According to the story, a merchant and sailor named Toricella was shipwrecked in the waters around Ugljan. He managed to save himself and swim to the shore in Ljokine Cove, and on that spot he decided to build a votive church. He dedicated it to Saints Cosmas and Damian, early Christian martyrs and physicians, in gratitude for his rescue.

THE ROOF OF THE SIMPLE LITTLE CHURCH WAS COVERED WITH BROKEN STONE SLABS

Although the shipwreck story cannot be historically confirmed, the name Toricella also appears in old documents. The little church is first mentioned on 6 August 1512 in the will of F. Toricella from Bergamo in Italy. In it he stipulated that a piece of land should be given for use to the priest who celebrates a sung Mass in the little church on the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian. According to the interpretation of don Marko Dokoza, a priest who for years led tours of Ugljan’s little churches as part of Open Doors Days, Toricella was only later identified with the seafarer from the shipwreck legend.

The original church was a very simple, square stone building, 4.8 metres long and 2.8 metres wide. Its walls were about 80 centimetres thick, and at the rear it had a lowered semicircular apse. The roof was covered with broken stone slabs, and there were two small windows in the side walls. The interior had a half-barrel vault, while the simple architectural details reflected the modesty and age of the building.

PAINTINGS DEPICTING SAINTS COSMAS AND DAMIAN AND THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY WITH THE CHILD

At the beginning of the 20th century the little church was significantly enlarged. A new nave, ten metres long and 3.8 metres wide, intended for gatherings of the faithful, was added to its front part. Today its interior contains an altar, pews and paintings depicting Saints Cosmas and Damian as well as the Blessed Virgin Mary with the Child. On the façade a small round window stands out, and above it a stone bell-gable with a bell made in the workshop of Jakov Cukrov in Split.

Saints Cosmas and Damian, to whom the church is dedicated, were twin brothers and physicians who helped the sick free of charge. Their feast day is celebrated on the 26th of September. For centuries that date held special significance for the inhabitants of Ugljan: according to records in the parish chronicle, numerous pilgrims from all the settlements on the island, as well as from the neighbouring areas, used to come to the little church on that day.

IN THE NEARBY HAMLET OF GUDUĆE YOU CAN ALSO SEE A UNIQUE MOSAIC BENCH

The tradition, of course, lives on today. Mass is still celebrated in the little church, during which blessings are invoked upon Ugljan sailors and ships all over the world. Thus this small place of worship has remained connected with the sea and seafarers, just as in the legend of its origin. The Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian on the island of Ugljan is also interesting as an excursion destination.

It is located in a peaceful cove, and a gravel road through a pine forest leads to it. In the nearby hamlet of Guduće you can also see an unusual mosaic bench created back in 2019 by the retired Božica Kliman, known as Boška. On its front side is a depiction of the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian itself, along with a magical sunset, a squid and a lighthouse — colourful reminders of the islanders’ unbreakable connection with the sea and fishing.

World.title: The 3,500 Year Old Settlement Found Near Split
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – There is a fascinating 3,500 year old settlement in the suburbs of Split, with archaeologists coming upon the remains of houses, ovens and ancient graves.

Split is well known as the second largest city in Croatia and one of the best-known tourist destinations. It boasts an exceptionally long and proud history, but many don’t know that in its suburbs lies a settlement that is even older than this Dalmatian gem. As Lana Mindoljevic writes for Putni Kofer, over more recent years, archaeologists visiting the settlement of Stobreč have been discovering remains of life from the Bronze Age, long before the arrival of the Greeks and the Romans. Stobreč is formally a suburban settlement of Split and a popular tourist area, but it has its own exciting history that many people simply overlook.

the remains of an ancient epetium

Stobreč has long been known to archaeologists as the site of ancient Epetium, or Epetion. However, extensive protective research that began back in 2024, the largest so far conducted at this site, has also opened a much older chapter of its history. According to the information available so far, the earliest finds date approximately to 1500 BC, and detailed processing of the material is still ongoing.

over 10,000 fragments have been found

In a scientific paper written by Marina Ugarković and Niko Romac, published on the Hrčak website, parts of Hellenistic defensive walls and a tower, a Roman road and drainage system, and late antique buildings are described. Among these layers, the remains of an earlier prehistoric settlement have for the first time been unequivocally confirmed. Already in the research covered by that paper, more than 100,000 fragments of objects and other movable finds from different periods were documented. The soil under Stobreč has proven to be a vast archive of life that changed and built upon itself here for centuries.

ancient homes and grave sites

Archaeologist Niko Romac also described finds of ovens, possibly intended for food preparation, and complete ceramic vessels: trays, cups and jugs. Precisely such objects bring the ancient inhabitants of Stobreč closer to us. Someone made them, took them in their hands and used them in everyday life. Based on traces of burning and the arrangement of the remains, researchers assume that the house was destroyed by fire. Among the particularly sensitive finds, the grave of a newborn in its floor was also recorded.

an archaeological park is being considered

These remarkable discoveries have also opened the question of the future of the very special site. According to the response of the Ministry of Culture and Media, a zone of approximately 3,000 square metres is currently being planned for the presentation of the archaeological heritage. On an additional around 2,500 square metres construction is possible, but it depends on the results of further research. The sensitive Bronze Age finds require special protection. The Ministry states that the ovens and the find interpreted as a threshing floor should be moved to the Archaeological Museum in Split, while the appearance of the settlement could be presented with three-dimensional models and virtual reconstructions. An archaeological park currently exists only as an idea, and time will show whether it will be realised.

Stobreč is located on a peninsula east of Split, near the mouth of the Žrnovnica. In the central part of the place there are sandy and pebble beaches, while towards the southwest the coast becomes rockier. Because of the beautiful beaches and the proximity of Split it is a popular summer destination, and the proximity of Perun and Mosor also opens possibilities for trips into nature. Interestingly, even the name of Stobreč itself preserves the memory of its long past. As the Croatian Encyclopaedia notes, archaeologist Frane Bulić etymologically linked the present-day name of the place with the name of Saint Lawrence, i.e. the Roman martyr Laurentius, to whom the local early Christian basilica was dedicated. In its apse a small church of Saint Lawrence was later arranged, later dedicated to Our Lady of Carmel. Along with the preserved remains of the ancient walls, this is another reminder that in Stobreč different periods of history can be encountered during a completely ordinary walk.

World.title: Croatia is Introducing a New Digital Customs System
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce a brand new digital customs system as of November the 1st this year, with the hope of making crossing the border more efficient.

As of the 1st of November 2026, the Customs Administration is introducing a new digital service called eObračun of customs duties in passenger traffic (eODPP). Index reports that this brand new service is intended for passengers who bring goods into Croatia, i.e. the EU, on which import duties are payable, and its aim is to facilitate and speed up border crossing.

how it works…

Via the new application, passengers will be able to check in advance whether there is an obligation to pay duties on the goods they are bringing in their personal luggage. The service also enables them to declare goods whose value or quantity exceeds the permitted limits and to pay online the customs duties and taxes calculated on the basis of the declaration. Goods can be declared up to five days, i.e. 120 hours, before the planned arrival at one of the international border crossings within the territory of Croatia.

Upon arrival at the border, a customs officer will check the declaration and the goods in a short procedure. If no irregularities are found, the import procedure will be quickly completed. The Customs Administration states that the application is designed to be intuitive, and the data-entry procedure for calculating duties has five steps.

no registration required

The brand new Croatian digital customs service will be available to all passengers entering the EU via Croatian road, railway, air and maritime border crossings. No registration is required to use it. The system is adapted for computers, smartphones and tablets, and will be available from the 1st of November 2026 here.

World.title: Croatia is at Back of EU When it Comes to Electric Car Purchases
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – Despite the global climb in people buying electric vehicles, Croatia ranked at the very back of the EU when it comes to electric car purchases.

The share of fully electric cars among new cars is growing around the world, and in many countries it has reached record levels. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this is clearly shown by the latest data from the international energy organisation Ember, which analysed car sales on global markets. Croatia is significantly lagging behind the other EU countries.

croatia is at the very back of the eu

According to Ember’s analysis, which tracks the share of fully electric cars (BEVs) among newly registered cars, Croatia recorded its own record during 2026, but despite that remained in last place in the European Union. From March to August such cars accounted for around 4.3 percent of all new registrations in Croatia. The data are based on rolling six-month periods because this presentation allows clearer tracking of trends.

The research covered 56 countries, while 49 of them are shown on the interactive chart, i.e. only those that achieved record shares during 2026. The difference between Croatia and the European leaders is extremely large. In Norway, which is not a member of the European Union, the share of fully electric cars reached as much as 97.8 percent, in Denmark 79.8 percent, in Finland 49.7 percent, in the Netherlands 42.8 percent and in Sweden 40.8 percent. The European Union average was 22.5 percent, more than five times higher than in Croatia. As for the EU members that are not shown on the chart, these are Poland and Romania, which did not achieve record shares of electric cars during 2026. However, both are ahead of Croatia. From March to August the share of fully electric cars among new registrations was 4.8 percent in Poland and 7.4 percent in Romania.

why is croatia lagging so much?

One of the reasons for the weaker sales of electric cars across Croatia could be their high price, especially in relation to average local purchasing power. That Croatian buyers are largely turning to used vehicles is also shown by data from the Croatian Vehicle Centre, according to which more used cars are imported into Croatia than new ones are registered, while the average age of passenger cars is more than 13 years. The European Commission in its 2026 report on Croatia also warns of the high costs of public charging of electric vehicles, problems with different charging systems and limited possibilities for home charging, especially for citizens who live in apartment buildings.

State incentives also play an important role; they are not awarded continuously but through occasional tenders. Available funds can sometimes be used up in just a few hours. Thus in 2024 citizens reserved all 15 million euros earmarked for subsidies in only four hours, after which the Environmental Protection Fund closed the tender. Such a system makes purchase planning more difficult because citizens cannot count on the constant availability of incentives.

large market differences

There are also significant differences among the large European markets. In France the share of fully electric cars was 30.6 percent, in Germany 27.5 percent and in Italy 8.3 percent. Germany and France have in recent years been moving towards an ever higher share of electric cars, while their penetration in Italy is considerably slower. Nevertheless, the Italian market is also recording growth, especially during 2026. Looking at absolute numbers, China is by far the world’s largest market for electric cars by the number of vehicles sold and is in a category of its own. According to Ember’s data, from January to August 2026 almost 4.46 million fully electric cars were registered there, which is almost half of the total of 9.33 million registered worldwide. In the EU in the same period around 1.65 million such cars were registered.

electric cars are conquering even emerging markets

The data show that the growth in the share of electric cars is no longer limited to developed European countries and China. Among the countries with high shares, Uruguay stands out with 40.2 percent, while in Thailand the share reached 28.8 percent and in Indonesia 24.2 percent. “Strong growth outside the USA and China was key to the continued growth in electric vehicle sales. Excluding the USA and China, global BEV sales rose by an estimated 45% in the period from January to August 2026 compared with the same period of the previous year,” the research states. At the same time, electric cars in some large countries still occupy a relatively small part of the market. In India their share is 7.4 percent, in Japan 3.3 percent and in Mexico only 2.1 percent.

the usa didn’t even make it on the chart

Ember particularly highlights the example of the United States of America, which did not even make it among the 49 countries with record shares of electric cars shown on the chart. After last year’s abolition of federal support for electric vehicles, their share among new vehicles fell to only six percent in the first eight months of 2026. Looking at everything in absolute numbers of electric cars sold the USA stands considerably better. From January to August around 640 thousand such vehicles were registered there, which puts it in second place in the world, immediately behind China. However, the American car market is so large that electric cars still make up a small part of total sales. According to Ember’s analysis, as many as 49 of the 56 observed countries now have a higher share of electric cars than the USA, and during this year alone 15 countries overtook it, among them Brazil, India, Italy, Malaysia and New Zealand.

electric cars and energy security

Ember emphasises in its analysis that the spread of electric cars affects not only the car market but also the energy security of states. According to the organisation’s estimates, electric cars in oil-importing countries from March to August this year replaced oil consumption worth around 20 billion dollars.

The authors of the research conclude that the electrification of transport can reduce states’ exposure to disruptions on the oil market and sudden changes in fuel prices. “Countries that invested in electric cars before this crisis are now better protected, and their example is being followed by an increasing number of other countries. Every electric car on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets, and as their number grows, so does protection against future supply disruptions,” the research states.

World.title: What’s Going on With the Potential Šibenik Airport?
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – The idea of a future Šibenik Airport sounds feasible and very reasonable, but it seems like there’s been more than a few spanners thrown in the works…

The feasibility study and the revision of the conceptual design were supposed to be completed by the end of July this year, but almost three months later there is no public confirmation that the documents have been finished. As SibenikIN reports, in the meantime, the issue of the planned airport’s impact on the habitats of protected bird species has also been raised.

At a joint thematic session of the parliamentary committees for tourism and for maritime affairs, transport and infrastructure, held on Thursday the 22nd of October, the operations of Croatian airports, investments, their financial sustainability and future development were discussed. Representatives of the competent ministries, airports and the aviation sector took part in the discussion, and among the topics were the seasonality of traffic, the development of regional airports and the need for better transport connections.

However, the official parliamentary report fails to mention the Heart of Dalmatia airport project at Pokrovnik, in which Croatia holds a majority ownership stake. Although this does not rule out the possibility that the project was mentioned in passing during the session, it was not singled out among the development topics in the official summary.

the documentation should have been completed by july

Back in June this year, local portal ŠibenikIN reported on the status of the planned airport project at Pokrovnik. At that time, Šibenik Deputy Mayor Danijel Mileta, referring to a report by the company Zračna luka Srce Dalmacije that had been submitted to the City as one of the co-owners, confirmed that the feasibility study and the revision of the conceptual design with technical details were in preparation. According to the announcements at the time, both documents were supposed to be completed by the end of July 2026.

However, almost three months after the announced deadline expired, no publicly published confirmation has been found that the documents have been finished and handed over to the client. Such information is also not available on the company’s official website. At the same time, on 30 December 2025 the preparation of the environmental impact study and the main acceptability assessment of the intervention for the ecological network was contracted, with an 18-month deadline, i.e. approximately until mid-2027. According to the information obtained from the month of June, a geodetic elaborate, a climatological study and a project for a meteorological station had already been prepared, while the procedure for obtaining special conditions for the station itself was still ongoing.

protected bird habitats could become a serious problem…

In addition to the questions of deadlines and documentation, an additional obstacle has appeared that could affect the future of the project. As ŠibenikIN wrote in July, in the process of amending the Spatial Plan of Šibenik-Knin County the question of the planned airport’s impact on the habitats of protected bird species was raised.

Particularly highlighted were the calandra lark, the short-toed lark and the stone-curlew, whose habitats could be threatened by the construction and use of the airport. In the spatial-planning documentation it was warned that, due to nature-protection requirements, it might be necessary to re-examine the location or the category of the planned airport. Such a warning doesn’t mean that the ambitious Šibenik Airport project has been rejected or that construction at Pokrovnik has been banned. However, it opens the question of whether the existing conceptual design will be acceptable from the point of view of nature protection and whether additional changes will be required. It isn’t yet known whether these warnings have affected the preparation of the documentation that was supposed to be finished in July.

the state is the project’s majority owner

The Heart of Dalmatia airport project is being developed by the company of the same name, in which the Republic of Croatia holds a 55 percent ownership stake, while the remaining 45 percent belongs to Šibenik-Knin County and five cities. Josip Skelin was appointed director of the company back in May 2025.

Interestingly, State Secretary of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure Tomislav Mihotić, who earlier participated on behalf of the state in the establishment of the company for the development of the Šibenik Airport, also took part in today’s parliamentary session on the future of Croatian airports. The Pokrovnik project has for years been presented as a possible contribution to transport connectivity and tourist development of this part of Dalmatia, but before any possible realisation a series of professional, spatial, environmental and financial questions still need to be resolved.

After the expiry of the July deadline for the key documentation, questions now remain open as to whether the feasibility study and the revision of the conceptual design have been completed, how much money has so far been spent on the project, what its current status is in the state transport plans, and whether nature-protection requirements will lead to a change in the planned location or category of the airport.

World.title: After Decades of Decay, Rijeka Torpedo Launch Station Will Rise Again
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – Following years of decay, the famous Rijeka torpedo launch station will be given back its full glory and turned into a tourist site.

Rijeka has an exceptionally rich industrial history, and one of its most important monuments is located on the western part of the city waterfront, in the former Torpedo factory complex. As Ivana Vasarevic writes for Putni Kofer, right next to the sea, stands an unusual reinforced-concrete structure – the historic torpedo launch station. This is the exact place where weapons intended for navies around the world were once tested. After very many years of deterioration, this building, protected as a cultural asset of Croatia, will finally receive the restoration it deserves. The current plans also include transforming the entire surrounding area into a new tourist attraction.

turning the clock back to the 1860s…

Commons/Muzej Rijeka

Sea salt, waves and weather over the decades seriously damaged the ramp, so the conservation department as early as 2019 ordered urgent protection measures. Fortunately, it was decided that the launch station would not be demolished and replaced by a replica, but that the original structure would be preserved. Works should begin in the last quarter of 2026 and be completed during 2027.

The answer as to precisely why this structure is so historically significant takes us 160 years into the past, when an invention that changed naval warfare was born in Rijeka. During the early 1860s, Rijeka native Giovanni Luppis was developing the idea of a defensive weapon with which enemy ships could be stopped before they approached land. He called it the “coast saver”, but he lacked the technical knowledge and funds for its realisation.

rijeka torpedos were sought after around the world

He presented the idea to Robert Whitehead, a British engineer and the former manager of the Rijeka Technical Institute. He then developed a torpedo resembling a metal fish that moved independently under the surface of the sea. The first usable torpedo was successfully tested in Rijeka in 1866, and nine years later the Institute became the R. Whitehead & Co. factory, the first torpedo factory in the world.

Rijeka torpedoes soon became sought after around the world. They were ordered by Great Britain, France, Italy, Germany, Sweden, Japan, Russia and many other countries. The factory expanded its business, opened plants abroad, and production in Rijeka continued until 1966. Of course, before delivery to customers the torpedoes had to undergo a series of demanding tests. That is precisely what the launch stations were used for, from which trial launches were carried out and the behaviour of the torpedoes in the sea was monitored.

The first launch ramps were wooden structures from the 19th century, and over time they were replaced by a more solid reinforced-concrete station. According to data from the Museum of the City of Rijeka, it was built in 1930, and four years later a section intended for testing torpedoes launched from aircraft was added. Thus the station served for simulating the launch of torpedoes from ships as well as from the air: Rijeka, after all, did not yet have its own airport at that time.

Although production ceased long ago, the ramp still reminds us of the time when Rijeka was an international centre of technological innovation. Its importance goes beyond local frameworks because it testifies to the development of an invention that changed world naval history. In addition to the restoration of the launch station, plans also include the arrangement of the Torpedo Visitor Centre. As the portal Fiuman recently reported, it would exhibit full-size torpedoes, their parts and technical elements, while a special virtual room would bring the history of this Rijeka invention closer through multimedia content.

transforming history into a tourist site

As for the architectural solution, it is conceived as a combination of industrial heritage and contemporary design. The façades of the centre should be adorned with archival photographs and technical drawings of torpedoes, while steel elements would in shape recall the plating of a submarine. Along the waterfront a promenade with a beautiful view of Kvarner and the launch station is planned, a viewpoint reached by stone steps, as well as a small square and the surrounding public areas.

World.title: Capped Prices Introduced for Pula Advent This Year
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – Good news for lovers of festive cheer as capped prices will be introduced for certain food and drink items sold at Pula Advent this year.

The City of Pula has decided to limit the prices of the most popular products at Advent stalls in order to make them more affordable. A city decision has set maximum amounts for part of the hospitality offer during the upcoming Advent. Index reports that rather unsurprisingly, this decision has been welcomed by all.

a new (capped) price list for pula advent

Under the new rules, the price of a hot dog, hamburger and bakalar (dried cod) will be limited to five euros. Mulled wine, hot chocolate and cocoa may cost a maximum of three euros, while the maximum price for tea and water will be two euros. The sweet offer, which includes fritule (fritters), pancakes and Christmas cookies, is also limited to three euros per portion. Deputy Mayor of Pula Siniša Gordić explained how the system will work. “It is about one product that caterers must have on offer, as stated in the public call. For the entire rest of the offer, if they want to have something additional, they can set the prices themselves if there is interest,” Gordić said. He added that a minimum quantity or portion has also been defined for the products with limited prices.

Danijel Britvić, who has been taking part in Pula Advent for years, considers the idea good, but warns that the quality of ingredients affects the final price. “Hot dogs are 80-gram items, an ordinary frankfurter that I already had for five euros in a large bun. We have a 100-gram sausage and it cannot cost five euros, but six or seven. I will have the same prices as last year, but I will also include a hot dog at the set price in the offer,” Britvić said.

What is new in Pula has already been a proven model in Poreč. There, part of the offer has been sold at limited prices for years, which has proven to be a successful practice. “We’ve adjusted those prices over the years according to market conditions, but always so that they remain within a framework that allows each of us to go out with friends to Advent, treat everyone to a drink and eat something, without it being too great a financial burden and so that they come back again,” said Ajna Temimović from the City of Poreč.

The first test of the new decision by the Pula city administration will be visible soon, as the public call for the lease of Advent stalls ends at the end of October.

World.title: Anušić: Ukraine is Showing the Bravery Croatia Did in the 1990s
World.content:
October the 24th, 2026 – Speaking in Vukovar, Defence Minister Ivan Anušić has stated that Ukraine is currently going showing the bravery Croatia did back during the 1990s.

Defence Minister Ivan Anušić spoke in Vukovar about how Croatia must continue to help Ukraine because its defeat or the imposition of an unjust peace could lead to a new war on the borders of the European Union.

“Such heroism, sacrifice and respect for one’s homeland is what we also saw in our Homeland War back in 1991. That is why we must continue to help the Ukrainian people who, unfortunately, are going through the same wartime fate we experienced in the 1990s. Because if Ukraine loses this war or if it’s forced into an unjust peace, we’ll once again have war on our own borders,” Anušić said, according to a statement from the Ministry of Defence (MORH). Index reports that the minister made the remarks at the premiere of the documentary film “Glory to the Heroes”, which tells the story of two Ukrainians of different political convictions who fought and died for the independence of their country.

After the premiere, Anušić took part in a panel discussion on the Homeland War and the war in Ukraine. Alongside him were Croatian defenders Fanika Janko and Ivan Lukić Zolja, as well as the documentary’s director Alceo Marti. The conversation was moderated by Goran Rotim.

Anušić stressed that Croatia, because of its own wartime experience, particularly understands what the Ukrainian people are going through today. “There are a great many parallels between our Homeland War and the war in Ukraine. The Croatian people, who themselves lived through the sufferings of war, have a special understanding for the Ukrainian people. Just as Vukovar in 1991 put up heroic resistance against a superior Greater Serbian aggressor and became a symbol of Croatian freedom, so Ukraine today is heroically fighting against Russian aggression and keeping the war away from the borders of the European Union,” Anušić said.

He added that Vukovar, because of its defence in 1991 and the suffering it endured during the Homeland War, is a particularly appropriate place for the premiere of a film about Ukrainian defenders. Speaking about the two Ukrainians whose destinies are shown in the documentary, Anušić emphasised that, despite their different political views, they defended their country together.

“One of your interlocutors in the film says that war brings out the worst in people, but it also brings out the best. Two young men who were politically on different sides, when the freedom of Ukraine was at stake, then had only one side – their common struggle for Ukraine,” the minister concluded. He added that similar stories of courage, sacrifice and unity can also be found among Croatian defenders from the Homeland War.
