World.title: If these walls could talk: Why Cape Town dressing room will haunt Aussies
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket If these walls could talk: Why Cape Town dressing room will haunt Aussies Daniel Brettig October 26, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Town: Something enduring about the cricket grounds in South Africa is they tend to be little changed from previous visits. So there is a distinctly eerie feeling about returning to Newlands for the first time since the infamous 2018 “sandpapergate” Test match. Some typical early cloud obscures Table Mountain on the morning I arrive, but the cricket ground itself is much more open a few days out from the third Test, before either team has arrived to practice. Loading That means when I walk in at the Kelvin Grove End, most doors are open. I wander through the Western Province Cricket Club stand and out onto the field. A few metres to my left is the gate leading up to the visitors dressing room, and I follow it curiously. The steps adorned with fake grass had their own moment of infamy in 2018, when David Warner walked up them after his first-innings dismissal by Kagiso Rabada, accompanied to one side by the guest of a WPCC member who abused him all the way. That person would later be ejected from the ground.



That enclosure and its red seats are also where the travelling media sat to interview Steve Smith before the game. Tellingly, he spoke of a state of mental exhaustion. “I didn’t feel I was hitting the ball that well [during the home summer], but my mind was in a good place,” Smith had said. “Maybe now my mind is not in as good a space as it was, but I feel now I am hitting the ball better.” Cameron Bancroft (left) and Steve Smith face the media after the Cape Town cheating scandal in 2018. Getty Once I get to the top of those stairs, more steps lead to the Australian dressing room, where so many fateful events took place eight years ago. The door is opposite the team viewing area, a small box perched between the two stands, where cameras picked up then-coach Darren Lehmann using a walkie-talkie to communicate with the team via squad member Pete Handscomb, after the Newlands big screen had shown something was up with Bancroft. In 2014, it was the place where Shane Warne took a few daytime naps during an all-too-brief spell as part of the team coaching staff.





The smallness of the rooms also means the corridor outside them became an impromptu meeting place. I walk along that corridor conscious that these are the places where Steve Smith chose, with Bancroft, to walk over to the media centre and take part in a press conference that played a major role in seeing them both banned from the game. Countless other discussions no doubt took place, and from seeing the space (or lack thereof), I get a sense of how it was possible for some to know more than others that infamous day. Since 2018, there has been some renovation of the area. The shower and toilet room next to the main dressing room is new and roomier than its predecessor. The walkway to the changerooms at Newlands cricket ground in Cape Town (main) and the screen at the ground (top right), as they appear today, and the ground as it looked during the 2018 Test match between South Africa and Australia (bottom right). Daniel Brettig x2 + Getty There's also a small dining room in the area, before the corridor leads out to the back entrance. It's here that I find the local security man, who kindly but firmly escorts me out and back down the stairs, past the signs outlining the players, support staff and match officials who will be permitted in the area during the game. After that, I walk around the Newlands concourse towards the media centre, which offers similar views to the “clock radio” press box at Lord’s. A new corporate and office space was built alongside it a couple of years ago, and beneath the building is a small cricket shop. The shop assistant and I share a joke about how much sandpaper he sells, before he tells me that the pitch for this week won’t be as grassy or seam friendly as those in Durban and especially Gqeberha.



Then it’s up to the media centre, which in 2018 also served as the press conference room for Smith and Bancroft. It’s had a considerable glow-up since then, doubling as a corporate events space, but it is still possible to remember how it all looked and felt in those heavy hours when Australian cricket lurched into crisis. Related Article Australian cricket New ball warm-up for Renshaw, as Green eyes No.5 spot on return from ‘bizarre’ injury Australia are staying well away from the Cullinan Hotel near Cape Town's waterfront, their base in 2018. But for Smith, captain Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and other members of the travelling group who were present eight years ago, it will be an odd experience at times to walk that same corridor and sit in those same rooms in a Test match. It should also be a moment to realise how far they have come, and how much more perspective exists in the current side. Unquestionably, there is pressure on this week to perform, exacerbated by the sheer scale of the team's defeat at St George's Park. Whatever happens, the Australian Test team is highly unlikely to lose its moorings in quite the same way. Nor, one suspects, will the Newlands crowd . The ghosts of 2018 might be a little more vocal. World.title: The feud threatening the $88 billion Ray-Ban family fortune takes a twist
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesBillionaires The feud threatening the $88 billion Ray-Ban family fortune takes a twist Tom Haynes October 26, 2026 — 7:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Behind the sleek sunglasses and effortless glamour inextricably linked with the Ray-Ban name lies a messy family feud that is anything but stylish. “My father gave us everything, but not love,” declared Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, one of the heirs to the family empire in a podcast interview with Italian rapper Fedez that invited comparisons with the TV drama Succession. Leonardo Maria del Vecchio with his girlfriend Kornelia Ski earlier this year at the Cannes Film Festival. WireImage As well as the revelations about his relationship with his father, the eccentric 31-year-old billionaire also boasted of sleeping with more than 2000 women and owning two yachts, while joking that he had debts of around €1 billion ($1.6 billion). But it is his increasingly public dispute with Francesco Milleri, the man his father entrusted with running Ray-Ban, the Paris and Milan-based group EssilorLuxottica, that could have the most profound consequences.



Related Article Billionaires ‘Obsessed’: The reclusive billionaire heiress who can’t stop getting richer Leonardo Maria has accused the chief executive of losing his way, blaming him for a collapse in the company’s share price. In an interview he said of Milleri: “When he was delivering results, I was his biggest supporter.” He also criticised the company’s lack of vision and said Milleri should be more concerned about the share-price slump. “The momentum from my father has run out,” he said. In his resignation letter, Leonardo Maria said: “This is not the Luxottica I grew up in.” Milleri subsequently described the public disagreements as “useless and unfounded”.



Yet his attack on the boss chosen by his father, Leonardo Del Vecchio, is awkwardly timed. Shares in the world’s largest eyewear company surged around 15 per cent last week after better-than-expected results, strengthening Milleri’s position ahead of his reappointment next year. It is the latest twist in a bitter battle over a family fortune worth more than €55 billion ($88 billion), with eight heirs fighting over their inheritance while the business at its heart continues to thrive. “There is always some governance drama,” is the understated assessment of Piral Dadhania, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets. He recalls boardroom tensions under its founder, during its merger with French lens-maker Essilor in 2018 and after his death four years later. But the latest dispute is unusually personal.



During his podcast appearance, Leonardo Maria described growing up surrounded by private jets, chefs, nannies and bodyguards, and recalled being thrown out of the family home at 18 over a girlfriend and discussed his past drug use. His romantic exploits were equally colourful: he boasted that the 2000 women he had slept with were mostly won over by singing Enrique Iglesias’s Hero. Leonardo Del Vecchio with wife Nicoletta Zampillo wife in 2011. Getty It is a remarkable portrait of the gilded life of the son of the self-made entrepreneur who rose from a grim early life in a Milanese orphanage to become one of Italy’s richest men. Del Vecchio founded Luxottica in 1961, transforming a small spectacles workshop in Agordo, in the Veneto region of north-east Italy, into a global giant through acquisitions and licensing deals.



Related Article Medicine She lost her sight. Her Wall Street billionaire father bet on a daring new treatment The merger with France’s Essilor in 2018 created a business with brands including Ray-Ban, Oakley and Persol. But his complicated personal life would prove harder to untangle after he died of pneumonia in 2022. Ownership of Delfin, the Luxembourg holding company that controls roughly a third of EssilorLuxottica, was divided into eight equal stakes. His six children each inherited 12.5 per cent, alongside widow Nicoletta Zampillo and her son from a previous marriage, Rocco Basilico.



Strict rules governing major decisions have since left the heirs struggling to agree on dividends, ownership and Delfin’s investments. Leonardo Maria attempted to buy the stakes of two siblings, Luca and Paola, for around €10 billion earlier this year, potentially tripling his holding to 37.5 per cent. Milleri supported the plan, but Romolo Bardin, the Delfin chief executive, opposed the holding company’s involvement in financing it. The proposal failed to win sufficient backing. Within months, Leonardo Maria had turned against Milleri. He resigned as EssilorLuxottica’s chief strategy officer and Ray-Ban chairman in August, complaining that management had grown distant from employees.



“This is not the Luxottica I grew up in,” he wrote in his resignation letter. Milleri said in a recent interview with Italian newspaper La Repubblica that he was “deeply sorry” about Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio’s departure from the company. Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in a Ray-Ban eyewear store in Rome. Bloomberg “I tried to help him in every possible way, including during the complex transaction involving the purchase of Delfin shares,” Milleri said. “I understand his situation and hope it can be resolved soon. My affection for someone I have known since the day of his baptism cannot change, even during such an emotional period.” He also defended the company’s performance under his leadership, which added €3 billion in sales this year.



“Twelve years ago, it was mainly an eyewear company generating €7 billion in revenue and employing 85,000 people,” he said. “Today, we are approaching €30 billion in revenue, with 220,000 employees and activities that span eyewear, vision care, medical technology and hearing solutions.” The reversal was striking. As recently as March, he had publicly backed Milleri as his father’s chosen successor. Leonardo Maria has spoken of promising to defend his father’s wishes as he stood by his coffin. Yet it was his father who entrusted Milleri with running the business. Alfredo De Massis, a professor of family business at IMD Business School and the University of Chieti-Pescara, believes the contradiction reflects a classic struggle between heirs who want control and a professional manager appointed to exercise it. Meanwhile, EssilorLuxottica’s fortunes on the stock market have taken a dramatic turn.



Shares soared last year as investors became excited about its partnership with Facebook owner Meta, which is turning Ray-Ban sunglasses into AI-powered devices capable of taking photographs, answering questions and translating conversations. Related Article Billionaires OnlyFans owner received $990 million windfall before his death But enthusiasm faded as investors worried that smart glasses would be less profitable than conventional eyewear, while Google and Samsung prepared competing products. Jelena Sokolova, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, says investors had allowed their excitement to get ahead of the company’s prospects. “I did see shares as overvalued last year, for instance, on all this AI optimism,” she says.



The subsequent sell-off wiped almost half the value from EssilorLuxottica’s shares at its lowest point, giving Leonardo Maria ammunition against Milleri. But Dadhania believes the chief executive has been unfairly blamed. “The core business has performed remarkably well,” he says. “My affection for someone I have known since the day of his baptism cannot change, even during such an emotional period.“: EssilorLuxottica CEO Francesco Milleri. Corbis via Getty Images Others remain cautious. Deutsche Bank warned this month that investors were still expecting too much from EssilorLuxottica, questioning the prospects of AI glasses. But Tuesday’s trading update offered Milleri a powerful response to his critics.



Sales rose 9 per cent to €7.49 billion in the three months to September, beating analysts’ forecasts. Its traditional eyewear and medical-technology business continued to grow, while sales of smart glasses and other wearable devices jumped 20 per cent. Milleri and Paul du Saillant, the deputy chief executive, said: “Quarter after quarter, our Company continues to demonstrate the strength of its unique model.” Sokolova says the company also benefits from a process far more dependable than the latest technological craze; people are living longer and more of them need glasses. ‘The momentum from my father has run out.’ Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio She argues that even if technology companies make smart glasses commonplace, customers will still want fashionable frames, just as luxury watches have survived the arrival of the Apple Watch.



For all the family’s disagreements, analysts see little immediate prospect of Leonardo Maria forcing Milleri from his position. EssilorLuxottica’s board has publicly reaffirmed its support for the chief executive, who has reshuffled senior management since the heir’s departure. Related Article Billionaires Ray-Ban billionaire heir details drug issues, says he slept with 2000 women as he escalates feud Asked whether Leonardo Maria could realistically challenge Milleri while the board supports him, Dadhania replies: “I don’t think so.” Leonardo Maria did question Milleri’s reappointment in 2027 in a September interview with Corriere della Sera and discussed finding a successor, although he also qualified this by saying: “Nobody has said Milleri must leave.”



Delfin has meanwhile reportedly explored buying back shares from some heirs, potentially reducing the number of beneficiaries from eight to six, easing the inheritance deadlock. Sokolova suggests the heirs may ultimately have to reconcile themselves to a more limited role, collecting the returns from their father’s business rather than directing its operations. For De Massis, the family’s greatest challenge, the real test of succession, is not deciding who gets the money. Rather, it is ensuring that the business survives the struggle “to create value for future generations”. World.content:
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek says parliamentarians can engage in “robust” debate without meanness or cruelty as MPs are urged to consider signing a civility pledge which had been backed solely by Helen Haines before she was attacked last week.

She told Seven’s Sunrise this morning that the attack on Haines had to be “a turning point” in how politics was done in Australia.

“It is really possible to have strong debate about issues without any censorship, and not be mean, and not be cruel, and not inflame things,” Plibersek said.

Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek. Alex Ellinghausen

She said it was incumbent on everyone in every sector to consider how they could be more decent to the people around them.

“It’s not just about politicians, of course it’s not. What we’re hearing is that teachers and principals and shop assistants and flight attendants and the kids who are reffing sport on the weekend are being abused just for doing their jobs. Surely, all of us have a role to play.

“In your own behaviour, as you’re going about your business, as you’re walking into a shop, or you’re getting impatient when you, you know, waiting in a queue for too long, just think: Can I do this better? Can I be kinder to the people around me?”

World.title: The Brisbane private schools that offer the biggest scholarships
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school The Brisbane private schools that offer the biggest scholarships Catherine Strohfeldt October 26, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Brisbane’s private secondary schools award almost 50 different scholarships – and like public sector excellence programs, they spark heavy competition. Across about 40 Brisbane independent and Catholic schools, two schools advertise up to 100 per cent tuition relief for academic scholarship recipients. Lourdes Hill College and Mount Alvernia College offer three-year scholarships for year 7 and 10 students. Lourdes Hill College is among two schools offering up to 100 per cent fee relief for scholarship recipients. Markus Ravik At Lourdes Hill, this would amount to roughly a $40,000 discount for a year 7 student, and more than $42,000 for a year 10 student, based on 2026 tuition fees and ignoring annual cost increases.



At Mount Alvernia College, a 100 per cent reduction on tuition fees translates to a cost reduction of about $32,000 for a year 7 student, and $36,000 from years 10 to 12. E-Shane Lee, the director of Brisbane tutoring company Lee Excellence, said students enrolled in his company’s scholarship test preparation classes were not solely driven by how much they could save. Along with parental school preferences, he said students were also motivated by “their own ambition to get into that school that they want”. Lee said the roughly three dozen students in his classes – which help prepare students for ACER and Edutest aptitude tests – wanted recognition for their efforts.



“I would say a lot of the students in our program are very self-driven,” he said. Lee’s students aimed for some of Brisbane’s most sought-after private schools, including Brisbane Boys’ College and Anglican Church Grammar School (Churchie). Brisbane private schools offering academic scholarships without published values Anglican Church Grammar School (Churchie)

Brisbane Boys’ College

Brisbane Grammar School

Clayfield College

Loreto College

Padua College

Somerville House

St Aidan’s Anglican Girls School

St Margaret’s Anglican Girls School

St Paul’s School

St Peters Lutheran College

Stuartholme School “Obviously, with some school fees rising at the moment, a lot of families see that a scholarship might be the difference between whether they want to go to a private school or not,” he said. Other students he tutored had their eyes set on highly competitive excellence programs at public schools, including Brisbane State High School, and the Queensland Academy for Science, Mathematics and Technology.



While these schools might not offer fee relief, the three Queensland Academy International Baccalaureate schools only offer selective entrance to students, while State High’s excellence programs function on a merit-based entrance model open to out-of-catchment students. E-Shane Lee’s company tutors students for scholarship tests. Lee Excellence “Entry to the school through the academic selective entry category is limited and heavily oversubscribed each year,” the school website said. Students entering through sporting or cultural excellence programs were required to adhere to strict requirements for their entire schooling journey, such as participating in the Greater Public Schools sporting competition events. Across almost 40 Brisbane private high schools, more than half offered no merit-based scholarships for new or incoming students – including Brisbane Girls Grammar School, All Hallows’ School, and Hillbrook Anglican School.



Among schools offering academic scholarships, only half published the percentage-value of their merit awards on their school websites. Brisbane girls’ school St Aidan’s Anglican College was among the schools offering the most scholarships, including an academic scholarship, specific merit-based fee relief, and bursaries. At St Aidan’s, the academic scholarship covered part of a student’s tuition fees – an all-inclusive fee for students from years 7 to 12 costing $31,992 each year. St Aidan’s offers many scholarships and needs-based awards, including one that covers 95 per cent of tuition fees. St Aidan’s Anglican Girls’ School Principal Toni Riordan said the school used its scholarship programs to bolster a “commitment to opportunity, belonging, and student growth”.



“This is reflected in our cultural scholarship and the recently established Creeth scholarship,” Riordan said. “These programs help expand access to a St Aidan’s education for students who will benefit from, and contribute to, our community, and particularly recognise character, potential, and alignment with the values of the school.” St Aidan’s Anglican Girls School principal Toni Riordan. The Creeth award, which considers merit and financial need, was funded through a charitable endowment. It covers 95 per cent of a student’s tuition fees, as well as textbook, uniform, and term-time accommodation costs from year 10 until the end of year 12. For a year 10 student in 2026, dismissing annual cost growth, this would amount to a $91,000 reduction in tuition fees alone.



In some instances, whether a school offers a scholarship or not is influenced by what education body owned the institution and what interschool associations it was associated with. Related Article Private schools The Brisbane schools parents pay thousands before students pick up a pencil For example, low-fee schools governed by Brisbane Catholic Education did not offer scholarships, although families experiencing financial hardship could apply for bursary support. Meanwhile, schools within the Associated Independent Colleges (AIC) sporting collective were banned from offering awards that could allow them to poach from competing schools’ teams. Among the six schools on the list were St Peters Lutheran College, Padua College, and St Patrick’s College, in Shorncliffe.



Other schools offered numerous culture, sports, and specific excellence scholarships, spanning from music and sport, to debating and chess – offered at St Joseph’s Nudgee College, Brisbane Boys’ College, and St Joseph’s College, Gregory Terrace (Terrace). Entry deadlines for ACER and Edutest aptitude tests fall across February and early March 2027. World.title: My suburb loves Halloween, and one kid’s costume perfectly captured our current moment
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My family was putting the final flourishes on our front-of-house Halloween decorations when we reached a stalemate over two plastic skeletons. Our overriding philosophy has always been to prioritise cute over hardcore scary. Were those skeletal figures going to spook the youngsters? Our two daughters made the final call to demote the ornaments to the lolly table, giving any visiting kids some breathing room. Welcome to Salisbury, Queensland. We may not have a murky history of druidic sacrifice like our English namesake, but for one night a year we practically turn into Stephen King’s town of Derry, with old-fashioned scares at every turn – and free chocolate. Spidey and Harry Potter get stuck in. Eddie Ngaluafe The Ngaluafe family celebrating Halloween. Courtesy Eddie Ngaluafe The neighbourhood gets into the spirit of the celebration. Etuani Ngaluafe Depending on which road you take, the approach might send a shiver down the spine. We’re bordered by the dense scrub of Toohey Forest, so in the moonlight the eucalypts give off a Blair Witch vibe. With headlights to guide your journey through the dark corridor, you might catch a fleeting glimpse of something uncanny. Those toy animal tributes to roadkill can take on a startling aspect if you’re not expecting them.



Inexplicable things do sometimes happen in Salisbury. In late 2023, a vicious localised storm rolled in without warning, toppled our washing line and destroyed the trampoline. Trees and powerlines came down around the neighbourhood. The kids remember the unnatural howling noise, the rattling windows, and sleeping through a humid night without power. Salisbury’s suburban footprint is smaller than you would think. Markus Ravik The Croatian Catholic Centre on Henson Road. Markus Ravik Salisbury Recreation Reserve. Markus Ravik Don’t be fooled by Google Maps: Salisbury’s footprint is smaller than they’d have you believe. When you look at where people actually live, dispersed between industrial complexes, train tracks and a green corridor tracing the contours of Rocky Water Holes Creek, it’s quite enclosed. You either live in the irregular polygon on the east side of Orange Grove Road, or you hang your hat in the satellite of Rosebank Square. Salisbury was once dominated by World War II manufacturing. The War Industries Heritage Trail passes through roads named for their function, like Assembly, Chrome and Precision streets. Walk through there now and you may spot the distinctive saw-tooth roof architecture of the era, alongside the unmistakable progress of gentrification, with new apartments going up, and an espresso bar in a building that once made munitions. Reload Espresso Bar occupies a former World War II munitions factory. Markus Ravik



Time for a coldie at Hiker Brewing Co. Markus Ravik Le Boulangerie Amour Fou. Markus Ravik Northsiders enjoy banging on about their local food culture as if it were definitive. But there are no less than five cafes in my suburb, each with their own strengths, identity and take on coffee. One even roasts their own beans. There are craft breweries, several bakeries (from French fusion to Sri Lankan), and an old-school butcher shop. You can get pizza, American-style barbecue, and just-like-homemade Indian tiffin meals. Order a halal snack pack at Kebabland or Billy’z Kebabs, and eat it next to a hungover uni student. My suburb punches well above its food division. It was a Facebook thread on the local grapevine page that got us started with Halloween. It may have been in the wake of social distancing restrictions relaxing in 2021. I put our street name down in the comments and drove to the local supermarket for bags of fun-size treats and last-minute decorations. We’ve been locked in ever since. I see more houses joining in with every passing year. You see children dressed in the typical costumes of superheroes and Disney princesses, but my favourite costume was from two years ago: a prescient kid knocked on our door dressed as the dreaded Cost-of-Living, complete with an $18 bottle of olive oil. Scarier at night: Toohey Forest. Markus Ravik



A war memorial. Markus Ravik A burnt-out building in the former Rocklea Munitions Works. Markus Ravik The weirdest house we have ever visited had a woman looking banged up, trapped in a cage and pleading for help. Dark stuff – until she offered you lollies. A parent at another house had his slasher tropes mixed up: wearing Jason’s mask while carrying a Leatherface chainsaw and dressed in Michael Myers’ trademark blue coveralls. While I disapproved on the grounds of film fidelity, kids were petrified and loving it. Horror is often a metaphor for something: usually an anxiety that gets distilled into the supernatural. I think we celebrate Halloween as a Salisbury community because we share a collective understanding that it is hard yakka raising kids. Related Article Life in the ’burbs My suburb was famous for car yards. Now we have coffee, culture and big plans for the future We’re all living in tough times with lots of uncertainty. Social support networks aren’t what they used to be, money is tighter than ever, and it’s easy to feel isolated. Halloween might seem pretty naff to some people, but for our family it is a small way to invite people into our home, to share and to have a good time as the year starts to wind down. Sometimes these small acts can help anchor you to something and make you feel like you belong somewhere. So, if you find yourself in Salisbury after dark on All Hallows’ Eve, you may knock on a weatherboard house that looks like all the others. If you’re greeted by a couple in matching Mr and Mrs Potatohead costumes, hello and welcome! Take as many mini-packs of Nerds as you like – and happy Halloween.

World.title: ‘It is ours’: The far-right Israeli settlers who want to build homes in Gaza
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Simhoni Forest: While many Palestinians dream of escaping the ruins of Gaza, Israeli Tchiya Chaim cannot wait for the chance to move there – and take her 11 children with her. For the past week, the settler activist and hundreds of comrades have been living in an outpost in southern Israel, just a few hundred metres from the Gaza border. Working quickly overnight to avoid detection, they established what looks like a squatter campsite with rows of tents, tarpaulins, demountables and caravans. There is also a jumping castle for young children and a classroom lined with religious texts. They have called the encampment Halutzei Aza – “the Pioneers of Gaza”. Settler activist Tchiya Chaim says Israel should re-establish settlements in the Gaza Strip. Matthew Knott “God willing, we will stay here until the government will take this settlement and put it into Gaza,” says Chaim, a member of the controversial Nachala settler organisation led by Daniella Weiss, known as the godmother of the Israeli settler movement. “It’s part of Israel, and we are going back there. On a basic level, it is ours.” And what should happen to the two million Palestinians who live there? “They have so many places they can go,” she responds with a grin. “For example, Australia. Such a big place. Don’t you have room for them?” As we speak, children run around wearing T-shirts saying “Gaza’s Jews”.



Chaim speaks glowingly of Gaza as a place of tranquillity and natural beauty, not mentioning the fact that most of its buildings have been destroyed or damaged during Israel’s war against Hamas, which killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. Locals there speak of rodent infestations and infectious diseases running rampant amid the rubble. The Pioneers of Gaza have nestled themselves between Kfar Aza and Nahal Oz, two of the kibbutz communities that came under brutal attack by Hamas on October 7, 2023. It’s a vivid display of the competing ideologies at the far ends of Israel’s political spectrum. The kibbutzim are famously left-leaning, pro-peace and secular; the Pioneers of Gaza and its supporters are right-wing, mostly religious, and committed to establishing a Jewish presence across all of what they call Greater Israel. A banner welcomes visitors to the Pioneers of Gaza community. Matthew Knott In the West Bank, settlers commonly use hastily built outposts to establish a foothold that later becomes a more developed and permanent community – despite the settlements being regarded as illegal under international law. This one, inside Israel’s 1948 borders, is designed as a way station to the Gaza Strip. Its arrival just days before Israelis vote in their first election since 2022 sends a message from the settlers that they want this to be a priority for the next government. ‘[The Palestinians] lost the war and when you lose you have to face the consequences. Relocating is the least they could do.’ Rabbi Duv Fendel The Nachala settlers had no permission to set up their camp in the forest, which is controlled by the Jewish National Fund, a major charity. But authorities are showing no haste in moving them on. When we visit, there are a handful of police at the scene watching passively. Eventually, the officers politely ask someone from the camp to join them for questioning at the station. When the settlers decline, they quickly give up. “We’re working together,” Chaim says, evincing no concern at being evicted. Israel’s police force is controlled by the ultra-national National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, himself a radical right-wing settler.



The mayor of the nearby town of Sderot, a stronghold of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, has visited to express solidarity and support for the settlers’ cause. An election campaign billboard for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir in the city of Ramat Gan depicts handcuffed Palestinian prisoners and a Hebrew slogan reading, “Strong Ben-Gvir, Strong Israel”. AP Twenty-one Jewish settlements were built in Gaza between 1967 and 2005, before Israel dismantled them under a policy known as the unilateral disengagement. Israel evacuated 8000 settlers from Gaza and relocated a cemetery containing 48 graves, while retaining control of the strip’s sea and airspace. The policy was deeply polarising at the time, with critics arguing it would expose Israel to more terror attacks. Soon after the disengagement, the Iran-backed Islamist militant group Hamas gained power and began smuggling in rockets and building an elaborate underground tunnel network. Two decades later came the October 7 attacks, which killed an estimated 1200 Israelis. Rabbi Duv Fendel, who has travelled from Sderot to teach Torah classes to the would-be Gaza settlers, says: “It’s outrageous that the only place in the world that by law a Jew is forbidden to live is in the Gaza Strip. Uprooting the settlements was one of the most hideous crimes in Zionism, and they need to be restored immediately.” As for the Palestinians living there, he peppers his speech with comparisons between Hamas and the Nazis. “They lost the war and when you lose you have to face the consequences. Relocating is the least they could do,” he says. Rabbi Duv Fendel says it is disgraceful that Israelis are not allowed to live in Gaza. Matthew Knott



The activists at the camp say they speak for a large part of Israeli society, and they are correct. While not commanding majority support, resettling Gaza is not a fringe position either. A poll by the Israel Democracy Institute last year found 40 per cent of Jewish Israelis support Israeli settlement of the Gaza Strip. Two of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s most senior ministers, Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, are campaigning for re-election on a platform of returning Jewish settlers to Gaza. Both have been sanctioned by Australia and other Western nations for inciting violence against Palestinians. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘National suicide’: The election issue tearing Israelis apart “I want all of Gaza. I want Gaza to be ours, I want it Zionist, I want it secure,” Smotrich told a campaign event this month. Ben-Gvir told Time magazine in a recent interview: “If Israel wants to continue to live and not be destroyed, we have to capture all of Gaza ... Israel is a tiny country. We have to be wider, broader.” Defence Minister Israel Katz, a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said in July that he intended to set up three military outposts in northern Gaza, a move that has traditionally been a prelude to civilian settlements. When Eliyahu Aton saw a story about the Pioneers of Gaza encampment on Channel 14 – Israel’s equivalent of Fox News – he drove from his home 45 minutes away to offer his solidarity. Resettling Gaza, he argues, will improve Israel’s security and ensure an attack like the October 7 massacre can never happen again. He believes the kibbutzniks living nearby who still believe in the possibility of peace with the Palestinians are dangerously naive. Danny Rahamim, a leader of the Nahal Oz kibbutz, counters that the settlers are “crazy” for wanting to resettle Gaza. “That would be like poking two fingers in their eye,” he says.



Critics argue resettlement would stretch the Israel Defence Forces to breaking point, drain the budget and expose Israel to international opprobrium. Netanyahu has repeatedly insisted that Israel has no intention of permanently occupying Gaza or displacing its civilian population. US President Donald Trump’s peace plan states that “Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza”. This is why Aton, who served with the Israeli military in Lebanon in the 1980s, says Netanyahu needs ideologically committed coalition partners who will push him further to the right. The 63-year-old used to vote for the left-wing Labor Party until the early 2000s but is now backing Ben-Gvir’s Otza Yehudid (Jewish Power) party. “He knows how to treat the terrorists. He speaks our language,” he says. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict October 7 changed their lives. Now they are running for office Aton’s shift reflects a broader ideological trend in Israeli society accelerated by the October 7 attacks. Nearly two-thirds of Jewish Israelis identify now with the political right and a quarter identify as strongly right-wing, according to a study released this month by the Jewish People Policy Institute. Just 22 per cent of Israelis now identify with the left. Ben-Gvir is expected to win about eight seats on Tuesday (Israel time), up from the previous election. That’s a massive turnaround from 2020, when his party failed to win a single seat. Younger voters, in particular, have been rushing to his campaign events, and conservative towns like Sderot are plastered with posters of him in front of handcuffed prisoners. Ben-Gvir drew international condemnation, including from Australia, earlier this year when he was filmed taunting pro-Palestinian detained after trying to enter Gaza on a flotilla carrying humanitarian aid.

World.title: The developers, the courtrooms and the battle over what gets built in Sydney
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The developers, the courtrooms and the battle over what gets built in Sydney David Barwell October 26, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Record numbers of planning disputes are being fought in court as developers increasingly challenge council decisions and communities find themselves caught in the middle of battles over what gets built in their suburbs. A plan to demolish an affordable inner-Sydney boarding house for luxury homes, a coastal housing estate opposed by hundreds of residents and a 20-storey Blacktown office tower by developer Bathla were among hundreds of developments approved by the NSW Land and Environment Court in 2025 after initially being refused by councils. A concept image of a development approved by the court for 204 units across five buildings on Burelli Street in Wollongong. Wollongong Council A newly released review by the court revealed 1108 development-related appeals were finalised last year – an average of more than three cases per day and the highest annual total since published records began in 2006. An analysis by this masthead of 743 publicly available judgments found 706 appeals resulted in approval, including through court-directed conciliation, while just 37 were refused – a success rate of 95 per cent.



The cases highlight mounting tensions between the state’s push to increase housing supply, councils seeking to enforce planning controls and residents concerned about the future of their neighbourhoods. Among the most contentious approvals was the demolition of a 32-room Paddington boarding house, overturning a City of Sydney council refusal over the loss of affordable accommodation and the displacement of tenants. Other projects included an $80 million over-55s estate with 146 homes on coastal land in Yamba, a fast-food precinct featuring McDonald’s, KFC and Guzman y Gomez outlets at Kariong that generated hundreds of objections from residents, and a solar farm with more than 9000 panels in Deniliquin. The court’s review found 54 per cent of development appeals arose after councils failed to determine applications within statutory deadlines of 40 days for standard applications and 60 days for larger proposals. Under NSW planning law, applicants can appeal when applications are deemed refused because deadlines have expired.



A concept image for a development by the Bathla Group at 30 First Ave in Blacktown, which was approved by the court last year. Blacktown Council The figures have intensified scrutiny of councils after the NSW government introduced reforms to allow more housing in established suburbs and warned local authorities they risked losing planning powers if assessment times failed to improve. Latest Department of Planning data shows 67 per cent of development applications are being assessed within its timing expectations, but several councils are recording rates below 30 per cent, including Burwood, Strathfield, Willoughby, Lane Cove and Hunters Hill. Statewide, a total of 1635 development applications were refused by councils in 2025-26, with Canterbury-Bankstown topping the list at 161, followed by Georges River (87), Woollahra (86), Sutherland (82) and Ku-ring-gai (66). Planning Minister Paul Scully said delays were alarming during a housing supply crisis.



“Projects which fit within planning controls should not end up in the Land and Environment Court, wasting ratepayers’ money and adding thousands to the cost of new homes,” he said. “It’s disappointing that some councils are continuing to stand in the way of much-needed housing supply.” A concept image of a development approved by the court at 55-69 Chandos Street in St Leonards. North Sydney Council Woollahra Council defended the highest number of appeals in NSW in 2025 with 59, followed by Northern Beaches (41), Central Coast (40) Georges River (37) and Liverpool and Inner West, each with 36. Affluent eastern suburbs and lower north shore councils also dominated appeals relative to population. Woollahra recorded the highest rate, followed by Hunters Hill, Mosman, Waverley, Willoughby and North Sydney. Fairfield recorded six appeals, Camden six and Campbelltown eight.



University of Sydney urban planning professor Nicole Gurran said the concentration of appeals in wealthier areas could reflect the financial incentives associated with developing valuable land. “The more valuable the site, the more likely a developer is to push the envelope and propose something that might not otherwise be permissible under council planning controls,” Gurran said. Residents of a Paddington boarding house strongly opposed a redevelopment of the site, approved by the court last year. Nick Moir “Developers can then effectively engage in ‘decision shopping’ by appealing refusals in court in the hope of securing a more favourable outcome.” Woollahra Mayor Sarah Dixson rejected suggestions the appeal figures showed her council was disproportionately refusing applications, saying some proposals went well beyond existing planning rules.



A concept image of a development approved by the court at 169-171 Herring Road, Macquarie Park. Ryde Council “Every application is assessed on its merits, but there are a lot of applications which go far beyond the scope of council controls that are not appropriate,” she said. Dixson said recently introduced NSW government planning reforms that allowed greater building heights and density had increased the complexity of applications, making statutory deadlines harder to meet. She said the council preferred to resolve disputes through conciliation where possible, but acknowledged concerns about the lack of public transparency of the confidentiality of those negotiations. Tom Forrest, chief executive of property industry group Urban Taskforce, said lengthy legal battles could add tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees and holding costs, undermining a project’s financial viability and slowing the supply of new homes.



But community groups say the growing reliance on court appeals risks sidelining local knowledge about infrastructure and the effects of development in their suburbs. Dennis Mentzines of the Drummoyne Responsible Development Group cited a nine-storey waterfront proposal approved on appeal after Canada Bay Council rejected it. The development was lodged under the state’s new reforms for low- and mid-rise housing that permit larger buildings in areas previously restricted to lower-density housing. “Local councils have a very good understanding of their own unique infrastructure constraints – schools, roads and hospitals – and the impacts on the local area,” Mentzines said. “The courts are now looking at one-size-fits-all statewide planning changes across suburbs that are all completely different to one another.”



Local Government NSW has called for a review of deemed-refusal rules, arguing they can push disputes into court before councils have sufficient time to resolve technical issues or complete complex assessments. Across all its jurisdictions, the court finalised 1671 cases in 2025, up 6 per cent on the previous year. Other cases settled by the court included a rising number of tree disputes, which jumped 14 per cent to 154 over the 12-month period. World.title: If these walls could talk: Why Cape Town dressing room will haunt Aussies
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket If these walls could talk: Why Cape Town dressing room will haunt Aussies Daniel Brettig October 26, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Town: Something enduring about the cricket grounds in South Africa is they tend to be little changed from previous visits. So there is a distinctly eerie feeling about returning to Newlands for the first time since the infamous 2018 “sandpapergate” Test match. Some typical early cloud obscures Table Mountain on the morning I arrive, but the cricket ground itself is much more open a few days out from the third Test, before either team has arrived to practice. Loading That means when I walk in at the Kelvin Grove End, most doors are open. I wander through the Western Province Cricket Club stand and out onto the field. A few metres to my left is the gate leading up to the visitors dressing room, and I follow it curiously. The steps adorned with fake grass had their own moment of infamy in 2018, when David Warner walked up them after his first-innings dismissal by Kagiso Rabada, accompanied to one side by the guest of a WPCC member who abused him all the way. That person would later be ejected from the ground.



That enclosure and its red seats are also where the travelling media sat to interview Steve Smith before the game. Tellingly, he spoke of a state of mental exhaustion. “I didn’t feel I was hitting the ball that well [during the home summer], but my mind was in a good place,” Smith had said. “Maybe now my mind is not in as good a space as it was, but I feel now I am hitting the ball better.” Cameron Bancroft (left) and Steve Smith face the media after the Cape Town cheating scandal in 2018. Getty Once I get to the top of those stairs, more steps lead to the Australian dressing room, where so many fateful events took place eight years ago. The door is opposite the team viewing area, a small box perched between the two stands, where cameras picked up then-coach Darren Lehmann using a walkie-talkie to communicate with the team via squad member Pete Handscomb, after the Newlands big screen had shown something was up with Bancroft. In 2014, it was the place where Shane Warne took a few daytime naps during an all-too-brief spell as part of the team coaching staff.





The smallness of the rooms also means the corridor outside them became an impromptu meeting place. I walk along that corridor conscious that these are the places where Steve Smith chose, with Bancroft, to walk over to the media centre and take part in a press conference that played a major role in seeing them both banned from the game. Countless other discussions no doubt took place, and from seeing the space (or lack thereof), I get a sense of how it was possible for some to know more than others that infamous day. Since 2018, there has been some renovation of the area. The shower and toilet room next to the main dressing room is new and roomier than its predecessor. The walkway to the changerooms at Newlands cricket ground in Cape Town (main) and the screen at the ground (top right), as they appear today, and the ground as it looked during the 2018 Test match between South Africa and Australia (bottom right). Daniel Brettig x2 + Getty There's also a small dining room in the area, before the corridor leads out to the back entrance. It's here that I find the local security man, who kindly but firmly escorts me out and back down the stairs, past the signs outlining the players, support staff and match officials who will be permitted in the area during the game. After that, I walk around the Newlands concourse towards the media centre, which offers similar views to the “clock radio” press box at Lord’s. A new corporate and office space was built alongside it a couple of years ago, and beneath the building is a small cricket shop. The shop assistant and I share a joke about how much sandpaper he sells, before he tells me that the pitch for this week won’t be as grassy or seam friendly as those in Durban and especially Gqeberha.



Then it’s up to the media centre, which in 2018 also served as the press conference room for Smith and Bancroft. It’s had a considerable glow-up since then, doubling as a corporate events space, but it is still possible to remember how it all looked and felt in those heavy hours when Australian cricket lurched into crisis. Related Article Australian cricket New ball warm-up for Renshaw, as Green eyes No.5 spot on return from ‘bizarre’ injury Australia are staying well away from the Cullinan Hotel near Cape Town's waterfront, their base in 2018. But for Smith, captain Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and other members of the travelling group who were present eight years ago, it will be an odd experience at times to walk that same corridor and sit in those same rooms in a Test match. It should also be a moment to realise how far they have come, and how much more perspective exists in the current side. Unquestionably, there is pressure on this week to perform, exacerbated by the sheer scale of the team's defeat at St George's Park. Whatever happens, the Australian Test team is highly unlikely to lose its moorings in quite the same way. Nor, one suspects, will the Newlands crowd . The ghosts of 2018 might be a little more vocal. World.title: FENZ assessing ground after Southland scrub fire
World.content:
Fire and Emergency are assessing the ground after a scrub fire in Southland on Sunday afternoon.

Six helicopters worked with monsoon buckets to protect two communications towers in the Centre Hill area after Emergency Services were alerted to the blaze at about 4 pm.

Last night FENZ said helicopter pilots had done an excellent job to protect the telecommunications infrastructure and there was no immediate risk to people or homes in the area.

Crews were stood down overnight although high winds were expected to keep the fire burning.

Today MetService had a strong wind warning in place for Southland with severe gales expected to reach up to 120 km/h in exposed places.

However, a Heavy Rain Watch in place could see conditions ease in the area when it came into effect early Monday afternoon.

FENZ said on Sunday the expected rain could make it easier to contain the fire.

World.title: Missing 11-year-old found safe after amber alert issued
World.content:
Police say an 11-year-old that went missing in Hawera has been found safe.

An amber alert was issued, after the young girl went missing on Sunday afternoon.

D'Havland Phoebe Jade Laupama had left her home on Koromiko Avenue in Hawera about 4pm on Sunday.

Police said the girl had a neurological disabilities including restless leg syndrome, which causes extreme fatigue in her legs.

They said on Sunday she was likely to lie down somewhere and fall asleep or hide.

World.title: Enrolments closed, advance voting begins for 2026 Election
World.content:
Enrolments have closed and voting in the general election begins today, with party leaders among those casting their ballot on day one.

Candidates were calling for last-minute enrolments on Sunday, while the Electoral Commission acknowledged the Government's changes preventing enrolment right up until voting day would impact numbers.

As of Friday - with two days remaining to enrol - 92.4 percent of those eligible had done so. In the 2023 election 94.7 percent of eligible voters enrolled.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the Government was to blame if the 2023 enrolment figure was not reached.

"If we do not have at least enrolment equivalent to what we had at the last election, that will be an indictment on this Government, who have deliberately tried to disenfranchise people, particularly younger New Zealanders, who are less likely to vote for them," he said.

The Greens' co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the Government knew that stopping people from enrolling to vote in the two weeks leading up to election day would disproportionately affect young people, renters, Māori, Pasifika, and migrant communities.

"These are structural barriers and it doesn't have to be this way. No politician and no government should ever make it harder for anybody to engage in our democracy."

However, National leader Christopher Luxon and ACT leader David Seymour disagreed, saying enrolling was simple.

"You've seen the Electoral Commission bombard everybody with advertising. I think they've had almost a doubling of advertising around voter turnout and voter enrolment. It's pretty simple and easy to do," Luxon said.

Seymour added it was people's duty to enrol.

"If you take all the benefits of a free and democratic society, but you're not prepared to perform a task simpler than ordering a pizza on Uber Eats to be part of that society, I think that is dropkick behaviour," he said.

Seymour said low enrolment rates would be an indictment on people who choose not to enrol, not the Government, which had simply set a basic expectation.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407351970112

ACT and Labour respond to National's 100-day plan

National on Sunday released its 100-day plan, setting out the first actions it would take if re-elected.

As a prospective coalition partner, Seymour said he would not get into pre-negotiations and detail what ACT would and would not agree to.

"There are some things that will go ahead, others that won't. Just like the last three years," he said.

"What's clear is that we can work constructively together, and having the ACT Party there to curb some of the National Party's worst instincts, while also promoting positive, practical solutions to New Zealanders' problems, is a good thing."

Meanwhile, Hipkins dismissed the plan as a reheat of previous announcements.

Talk of boosting bipartisanship during leaders' debates culminated in a handshake between Hipkins and Luxon at one point, with the pair agreeing to sit down together within the first 100 days of the next term and hash out what big things they could work together on.

RNZ asked Hipkins whether there was any part of National's 100-day plan he could get on board with.

He said National had shown no interest in collaborating on things that matter.

"They've shunned every overture from the Opposition in the last three years to work constructively together on big issues. I think that's unlikely to change if they continue to be the Government."

Calvin Samuel/RNZ

Hipkins doubts Opportunity's Future Generations Commissioner

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong on Sunday announced her party would establish a Future Generations Commissioner to hold governments to account for the long-term impacts of their policies if elected.

Wong said it would stop short-term thinking and guide development of long-term national goals.

Hipkins said he would be open to having a conversation about it, but any commission must be more than "just talk".

He was sceptical of those sorts of organisations - pointing to the Productivity Commission and Families Commission - saying they came up with good ideas, but those could not go anywhere without political support.

"We have a history of setting up sort of think tanks, advocacy groups that don't really affect positive, meaningful change.

World.title: Large scrub fire threatens telecommunications towers in Southland
World.content:
Strong gusts of up to 100 km/h are expected to keep a scrub fire in Southland burning overnight into Monday.

Six helicopters have been combating the blaze in the Centre Hill area with monsoon buckets since shortly before 4pm Sunday in an effort to protect two nearby telecommunications towers.

In a social media post, Southland Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said there was no risk to people or homes and flames were likely be visible in northern parts of the region, particularly the Mossburn area.

"Pilots have done an excellent job in challenging conditions to protect the telecommunications infrastructure on Centre Hill.

"We expect a change in the weather overnight will bring more favorable conditions for containing the fire tomorrow, with rain forecast."

The crews had been stood down for the night and FENZ would re-assess the situation at first light.

World.title: Five people rescued after boat sinks near Auckland
World.content:
Five people have been rescued after a boat sank near Ponui Island east of Auckland on Sunday.

Police were alerted to a boat sinking east of the island in the Hauraki Gulf about 5.30pm.

An eagle helicopter located the group in the water before signalling a nearby boat to come and assist.

World.title: Hundreds gather to demand end to bottom trawling in Hauraki Gulf
World.content:
Hundreds of people gathered on Waiheke Island today to call for an end to bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf.

The conservation organisation Forest & Bird said the fishing method was contributing to the gulf's ecological decline.

More than 80 percent of people living around the gulf want it to be banned, according to national conservation advocate Bianca Ranson. She said the event, which was held on Oneroa Beach, reflected their frustration at the continued decline of the gulf.

"Bottom trawling is widely recognised as one of the most damaging fishing methods, dragging heavy nets across the seabed and destroying vital habitats that are slow to recover," she said.

"There is no future for sustainable fisheries without ending destructive fishing practices and transitioning to methods that can sustain our ocean's life, long term".

Hundreds of people gathered on Waiheke Island for the Ban Bottom Trawling event. Supplied

Ranson said it had become an election issue, with Forest & Bird calling on all politicians to listen to the vast majority of New Zealanders who want a living, thriving gulf.

"Overfishing, sedimentation, pollution, and climate impacts, combined with bottom trawling, are pushing species towards local extinction. We need strong action to restore the gulf."

Ranson hoped that the turnout had shown political parties how much support there was for stronger protection of the ocean.

"The people are on the side, and we just need the political will to make this a reality.

"The Hauraki Gulf is a microcosm for the rest of Aotearoa. If we can get this issue right in the gulf, and that's commitment to ending trawling, that starts with a phase-out and moving away from bottom-impact fishing, which destroys the benthic habitat and seafloor, and moving towards new technology, which is already available, and making sure that industry is brought along so that we can end trawling, but also have sustainable fisheries."

The event also included the unveiling of New Zealand's largest-ever Ban Bottom Trawling banner, measuring 15 by nine metres.

"It took many, many of us to unfurl it. And then we walked it out into the ocean, where we were surrounded by people on waka ama and kayaks who were also holding Ban Bottom Trawling signs. And then all of the boats in the bay behind us. So, yeah, just a really powerful kind of visual statement of the message from the people, not only here on Waiheke, but people who have sailed over here to be here with us today and people who have come over on the ferry.

"So the message could never be clearer with this banner, but also the voice of over 80 percent of people who live around the Gulf who want to see this destructive fishing method banned. So we hope that all politicians can see that loud and clear with the photos that we'll be sending through to you. And, yeah, let's get on with it.

"Our future generations are depending on this, and also the well-being of our ocean, with all of the pressures that it's facing at the moment."

World.title: Child critically injured in assault at central Auckland park
World.content:
A child is critically injured after being assaulted by a man at a central Auckland park on Sunday afternoon.

Hato Hone St John said two people were taken to hospital after the incident in Myers Park at 4.45pm.

One has been taken to Starship Children's Hospital with critical injuries.

An area around the children's playground was cordoned off by multiple police officers following the incident.

Police said a 20-year-old man was taken into custody over the assault.

Police erect a cordon around the playground in Myers Park in central Auckland after a serious assault. RNZ/Pretoria Gordon

Inspector Jim Wilson said the man was not known to the victim.

Wilson said both the victim and offender required medical treatment.

"This was an isolated incident, and there is no ongoing risk to the public."

St John sent two ambulances to the scene, as well as a rapid response vehicle and an operations manager.

In a social media post, Auckland Central MP Chlöe Swarbrick said she had been in touch with local police about the serious assault.

World.title: Kiwis crush Aitu to cap dominant day for NZ at Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
After a brief scare, the Kiwis have crushed the Cook Islands 82-16 to pick up their first win of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

The tone was set early with a fierce pair of challenges, but it was the Kiwis firing the first shots with two quick tries.

But the Aitu shocked the Kiwis with three of their own to take a lead and briefly send tremors through the Kiwis coaching box.

Esom Ioka's quickfire hat-trick gave the Cook Islands a surprise lead, but it wouldn't last long as the Kiwis clicked into gear and blew the Aitu away.

It took just three minutes for the Kiwis to get on the board, a crisp series of passes through the backs sending Jamayne Isaako away for the opener.

Just moments later, the Kiwis were in again through their other winger Ronaldo Mulitalo off a great ball by Casey McLean and it looked like things could get ugly quick.

But with the Kiwis looking set for a third, the Aitu, struck against the run of play, Ioka plucking a pass out of the air and streaking 90 metres away to send Rarotonga into raptures.

The Cook Islands went back to back in quick succession, Brad Takairangi putting it on an absolute platter with a cross kick to Ioka for his second.

Another stunning moment followed for Ioka, this time a 40 metre intercept to put his side in front.

With a sense of panic and urgency creeping in, the Kiwis reclaimed the lead through Isaako, converting his own try from out wide with a superb in-swinging strike.

Relief replaced the unease as Scott Sorensen ran onto a prefect Jahrome Hughes ball to restore an eight point advantage.

Tanner Stowers-Smith scored a double on debut for the Kiwis. Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz

More breathing space came after Tanner Stowers-Smith, on debut in his home city, rumbled his way over for the Kiwi's fifth.

With halftime approaching, the Kiwis struck again through McLean to take them to 36-16 at the break.

Usually known for his slick footwork, fullback Keano Kini instead took the direct route as he bust his way through the Cook Islands line to kick off the Kiwis scoring in the second.

Taking the ball flat footed 10 out from the line, Tanner-Smith displayed his dogged determination to bulldoze his way over for a double on debut.

Kodi Nikorima brought up the half century, before McLean showed why he is regarded as one of the best centres in the game right now, effortlessly weaving past two defender for his second.

With the result assured the Kiwis brought the razzle dazzle, Isaako completing his hat-trick after some enterprising attack.

Isaako capped off his fruitful afternoon with a third try to go with 13 conversions before replacement Te Maire Martin dotted down in the act of copping a high shot.

Driving in one final nail to the brave Cooks Island side, Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad ended the Kiwi's try scoring spree in the 79th.

A brave effort by the Aitu, but the Kiwis just a class above in Christchurch.

The double header with the Kiwi Ferns saw the two teams rack up 174 points and 32 tries in a dominant day for New Zealand rugby league.
